title: Here's What Apple Fixed in iOS 27.2.1 and macOS 27.2.1
content:
The iOS 27.2.1, iPadOS 27.2.1, and macOS 27.2.1 updates Apple released today fix a handful of security vulnerabilities. With the security fixes implemented, it's a good idea to update as soon as you can.


A bug with iMessage could let a remote attacker join a group chat to receive its messages, and another could let users see messages sent before they joined a group chat.

AirPlay and Bluetooth. A malicious Bluetooth device could pair without user interaction, and another bug could let a nearby attacker corrupt process memory. Several bugs could allow an attacker to bypass the rate limit on ‌AirPlay‌ pairing code attempts.

Apple credits itself on four of the vulnerabilities, so they were found internally.

addressed the eMudhra certificate vulnerability, adding protections for command-line tools.

title: Best AirPods Black Friday deals 2026: Our picks for Pro, standard AirPods and Max
content:
Macworld






Best Black Friday AirPods deals so far: U.S.
AirPods Pro 3: $199 ($50 off, MSRP $249) – but we’ve previously seen $169
Best Black Friday AirPods deals so far: U.K.
AirPods Pro 3:  £200 (£19 off, RRP £219) – we recommend waiting for a better price
PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 9, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy AirPods, with retailers competing to offer discounts across Apple’s earbuds and over-ear headphones. Previous sales have brought substantial savings on established models, clearance bargains on older generations, and even discounts on newly released AirPods. But the biggest percentage saving doesn’t necessarily mean the best buy: an older pair needs to be sufficiently cheaper than its replacement to justify missing out on newer features.
Last Black Friday, standard AirPods 4 briefly dropped to $69 in the U.S., while the noise-canceling version fell to $99 – an $80 saving. Even the then-new AirPods Pro 3 received a discount of around $30, while older AirPods Pro 2 reached approximately $139 before selling out. AirPods Max were available for around $400, roughly $150 below their regular price. U.K. savings were more modest, with AirPods 4 at £99 and AirPods Pro 2 at £169, although stock frequently ran out.
This year, we’d watch AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 for meaningful discounts, while remaining AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 stock could bring some of the biggest clearance savings. The recently released AirPods 5 may see smaller reductions, making it especially important to compare their price with discounted Pro models. Below, we explain which AirPods to choose and how the offers compare with previous discounts. For savings on Macs, iPads, Apple Watch and more, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Which AirPods should you buy this Black Friday?


AirPods Pro 3 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Pro 3 are especially worth considering if you want strong noise cancellation, a secure in-ear fit, or Apple’s hearing-health features. Their foam-infused ear tips help improve the fit, while an in-ear heart-rate sensor adds another reason to choose them over standard AirPods. Battery life is rated at up to eight hours with noise cancellation enabled.
For most buyers looking for noise-isolating earbuds, these would be our first choice. Older AirPods Pro 2 are worth considering only when the clearance saving is substantial.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has already slashed $50 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we expect the price to go lower. Hopefully by Black Friday they will hit their all-time-low of $169.
U.K. Black Friday price: In the U.K. there’s £19 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we recommend holding out for a better deal. 






AirPods 5 – Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 5 offer a lower-cost entry point and an open-ear design for people who don’t like silicone-tipped earbuds. They include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, alongside Transparency mode and Adaptive Audio.
Check which charging case you’re buying. The Wireless Charging Case package adds wireless charging, longer battery life, a Find My speaker, and volume adjustment by swiping the stems. It’s our preferred package when the price difference is small.
U.S. Black Friday price: We’ve not seen a discount yet on the AirPods 5.
U.K. Black Friday price:  No savings yet on the AirPods 5.






AirPods Max 2 – Best for over-ear listening

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Max 2 are the option to consider if you specifically want over-ear headphones. The March 2026 update introduced Apple’s H2 chip and improved noise cancellation, while retaining the premium design and a choice of colors.
We find them difficult to recommend at full price, so the size of the discount matters. Compare any offer with previous sale prices rather than judging it solely against Apple’s asking price.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has the AirPods Max 2 for $449.99, that’s $99 off. They could still go lower though. 
U.K. Black Friday price:  The AirPods Max 2 aren’t currently discounted on the U.K. Amazon store, but hopefully we will see some good savings towards the end of the month. 






Other AirPods – Buy only at a worthwhile clearance price

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 can still be worth considering, but compare them with the discounted prices of their replacements. A large reduction from an older model’s launch price can disguise a small saving over a newer, more capable pair.
Check the exact generation, charging case, condition, and seller before buying. For more help choosing, read our AirPods buying guide.
U.S. Black Friday price:  We aren’t yet seeing any savings we’d recommend.
U.K. Black Friday price:  You can get the AirPods 4 with ANC for £109 at Amazon – that’s only £10 less than AirPods 5, so we’d recommend waiting for that price to go even lower. 






Other headphones – Worthy AirPods alternatives

				
					

				
			
Beats




If AirPods aren’t in your budget, Apple also sells a line of Beats headphones and earbuds that offer many of the same features for a lower price, including the popular over-ear Solo 4 and PowerBeats Pro 2. We’ll also track headphone deals in our round-up of the best earbuds for iPhone and best over-ear headphones if you’d like to see deals on other brands.
U.S. Black Friday price:  There is $100 off the Beats Studio Pro and $70 off the Solo 4 at Amazon, but we expect to see more discounts later in November.
U.K. Black Friday price:  There is £64 off the PowerBeats Pro 2 and £50 off the PowerBeats Fit at Amazon, but we expect to see more discounts later in November.






Should you buy AirPods now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need AirPods immediately. But the sales now stretch across much of November, with some deals already live, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer is close to a model’s previous low, it can be worth taking: last year’s best deals frequently sold out, and we expect popular offers to go quickly again.
Previous sale prices provide a useful benchmark. We’ve seen AirPods Pro 3 reach $169, while AirPods Max 2 fell to $399 during June Prime Day. An offer above those prices may still be worth considering. Discounts on the Pro 3 can also narrow the gap with standard AirPods, making their extra features more affordable.
For AirPods 5, waiting for a discount makes sense if you aren’t in a hurry: they didn’t receive a significant reduction during October Prime Day. We favor the Wireless Charging Case package when the premium is small. With AirPods Max 2, we’d hold out for a substantial saving rather than pay full price.
Compare retailers as well as generations. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year.






AirPods deals to avoid
When shopping for AirPods, be cautious about older models priced too close to their replacements. Compare the offer with the newer model’s discounted price, rather than judging the saving against an old launch price. Check any conditions attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods, including required spending, contracts, or rebates.
Check the exact version, too. AirPods 4 were sold with and without Active Noise Cancellation, while both AirPods 5 packages include ANC. The Wireless Charging Case version adds features and longer battery life, so a lower price may mean missing out on useful extras. Also check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair.
Judge the price against previous offers as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.
Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Counterfeit AirPods can be advertised at prices far below those from established retailers. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.






How we choose AirPods deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.

title: Anker Launches Eufy Security Cam With Auto-Tracking Light
content:
Anker today launched the Eufy TrackLight Cam S1, which it says is the world's first outdoor security camera with an auto-tracking light for actively deterring intruders. The TrackLight Cam S1 is compatible with Apple Home when using the Anker HomeBase, so it can be used alongside other smart home devices in a HomeKit setup.




When a suspicious person is detected, the camera locks on and follows them with a light from up to 12 meters (40 feet) away. The light adjusts with distance, narrowing when someone is far away and broadening as they approach. The camera has 355 degrees of horizontal rotation and can track movement up to 87 degrees per second.

An optional tracking deterrence mode activates the light and a 105-decibel siren at the same time, plus there is a red and blue flashing light mode as an additional deterrent.

The camera records in 4K with 10x digital zoom and night vision to show strangers in the dark. There is a 120-degree floodlight that works alongside the TrackLight, and dual radars offer 180-degree detection up to 40 feet. A Family List in the app allows the homeowner to set known people, so they get a soft, welcoming light as they approach. The feature detects a known phone's Bluetooth.

There's a 15,000mAh battery and a 5.5-watt solar panel for continuous operation, and IP65 dust and water resistance offers protection from the elements. There is no built-in storage, and users will need to add a microSD card or connect to the HomeBase. No subscription is required.

Anker also recently launched its Window Camera E10, a 2.5K resolution camera with anti-reflection and 25 degrees of tilt. It's designed to be put in a window, covering a yard, driveway, or entry without needing to be outdoors.

title: macOS 27.2.1 Fixes eMudhra Certificate Flaw in Command-Line Tools
content:
The macOS Golden Gate 27.2.1 update Apple released today addresses the eMudhra certificate vulnerability, and Apple recommends users update to the latest software.


For Macs that run macOS 26 or macOS 15, Apple has released macOS 26.7.3 and macOS 15.8.3.

blocked the compromised certificates in Safari, Mail, and apps that use Apple frameworks in October to protect most users, but command-line tools like curl and git were still able to accept them. With macOS 27.2.1, command-line tools will no longer accept the certificates.

Prior to releasing the macOS 27.2.1 update, Apple offered instructions for those who wanted to protect themselves from the compromised eMudhra certificates when using command-line tools, directing users to manually remove the affected root certificates from their Mac's "/etc/ssl/cert.pem" file.

has those instructions available for users who are unable to update their Macs.

The compromised security certificates were issued by certificate authority eMudhra. An investigation launched by Mozilla found the certificates used private key values below 256, making them trivial to recover. Attackers could use the keys to create fraudulent certificates that appeared valid for any website.

macOS Golden Gate 27.3 beta, but with the fix also included in macOS 27.2.1, users won't need to wait until December for protection.

title: Agentic Siri is coming, and that’s just the beginning
content:
Macworld





Siri AI is just the beginning. According to the latest newsletter from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who is always dialed-in to the inner workings of Apple, the new CEO John Ternus is pushing to make Apple a bigger player in the AI space.
While he had great things to say publicly about Siri AI at the launch of iOS 27, he is apparently delivering a somewhat different message in private. He seems aware, Gurman said, of the fact that Apple’s AI offerings are far behind rivals and not moving ahead with the same urgency. In a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, Ternus pushed to accelerate the company’s roadmap and move quickly past the long-overdue improvements to Siri.
With the OS 27.3 updates, developers will finally be able to make their apps accessible to Siri, so that Siri can perform in-app actions and access their data, if desired. Along with on-screen awareness and personal context, it’s the final pillar of the advanced capabilities Apple first announced two years ago.
But the latest trend in AI is agents. What started with hobbyist software like OpenClaw has grown into consumer-ready products like Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet. These AI agents run continuously and somewhat autonomously, taking care of almost anything a person can do online or on their phone or computer. There are some concerns over privacy and safety, and rightfully so, but they have already proven to be very popular.
That is a big step beyond “tell Siri to take actions within apps” and it’s where Ternus would like to take things. Gurman said Apple could make Siri act more like an autonomous agent “as early as next year,” and notes that the company hardly has a choice–announcing such a major feature at WWDC in June would put Apple a year behind the principal players else in the AI space, at least.
Gurman’s report paints the picture of a CEO concerned not just with matching AI companies feature-for-feature, but recognizing the increasing role of AI in computer use in general. The general idea is that, over time, more of what we do on our computing devices will be handled not by typing, clicking, and swiping, but by a personal agent that can essentially use any software we want it to at our direction. If you’re a company like Apple whose strength comes from selling physical computing devices and creating the operating systems that runs on them, ceding that level of control to a rival company could be an existential threat.
creator: Macworld

title: Apple releases security updates: iOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3, and 18.7.12
content:
Macworld





Apple has released a set of OS updates aimed around security updates. For those on the latest version of iOS, that is iOS 27.2.1. If you haven’t or can’t update to iOS 27, there are updates to older versions that include these critical software updates: iOS 26.7.3 and iOS 18.7.12.
These updates are joined by similar updates for Apple’s other platforms: macOS, watchOS, tvOS, and visionOS. 
Apple’s release notes only says, “This update provides bug fixes and security updates for your iPhone.” This is the boilerplate text for security releases. Apple’s security releases page does not list any of these OS updates at the time of this writing. It will likely be updated shortly to enumerate the security vulnerabilities addressed.
As we wrote back in September, frequent operating system releases that fix dozens of security vulnerabilities are the new normal. The latest AI coding tools have gotten so good that they may it much easier to find and exploit security holes, but also much easier to find and fix them. The race is on, and we can expect more updates that fix a much larger number of security flaws to be a regular thing for at least a year or more.

title: macOS 27.3 increases security with changes to Full Disk Access
content:
Macworld





Back in October, Apple announced a major security change to macOS. The change involves Full Disk Access (FDA), a permission that, when granted to an app requesting it, allows that app to access protected sections of macOS, such as data caches, mail, backups, and more.
The change is coming in macOS 27.3, which has recently started its developer beta cycle and should be available as a public beta soon. As itspdfu points out in a post, users will need to make the extra effort to allow an app to have FDA. Users will have to go into System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access and add the app manually. Previously, the app would be able to add itself to the FDA list and the installer would instruct users to simply toggle on FDA for it.


macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.
When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb
— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 7, 2026





The reason for the change: AI. “As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” according to Apple in a developer blog post. “We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”
Itspdfu also states that macOS 27.3 introduces “‘Private Folders,’ a new folder-by-folder permission configured like Full Disk Access.” However, this feature doesn’t seem to be fully capable as of yet. 
The macOS 27.3 beta 1 for developers was released on November 2. The official release of macOS 27.3 is expected in December.

title: Apple Continues to Say Some AI Features Will Have Fees for Extra Usage
content:
Apple continues to advise customers that certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on its server-side Private Cloud Compute system have daily usage limits, with expanded access to such features to be "available for a fee in the future."


Apple has repeatedly mentioned these upcoming fees in press releases over the past several months, but it has yet to provide any specific details about timing or pricing. The company did confirm that expanded access to the features will eventually be included with select iCloud+ plans, rather than something available for a standalone fee.

Extra server-side usage for a fee will be available for Siri AI, Image Playground, the Extend and Reframe options in the Photos app, shortcuts created with natural language in the Shortcuts app, and more. Apple says daily limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other unspecified factors.

iCloud+ plans and prices in the U.S.:

  
50GB: $0.99/month

  
200GB: $2.99/month

  
2TB: $9.99/month

  
6TB: $29.99/month

  
12TB: $59.99/month

It is unclear if these prices will increase once the expanded AI access is included.

Apple having said that extra usage will be included with "most" iCloud+ plans seemingly rules out the 50GB plan for $0.99 per month receiving this benefit at a minimum.

Logic Pro

Apple last week updated Logic Pro for Mac with a new intelligent assistant feature that can help creators "navigate production workflows, start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project."


The intelligent assistant has a monthly usage limit, with expanded usage packs available to users with an active Apple Creator Studio subscription in the United States, Canada, Brazil, France, Germany, India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom. In the U.S., the usage pack is currently priced at $49.99 and valid for one year.

To purchase additional usage, choose Logic Pro from the macOS menu bar, choose Intelligence Features, choose Show Usage, then choose Buy More Usage.

support document, Apple says some intelligence features in Apple Creator Studio apps are powered by "third-party providers." For the Logic Pro assistant, it says the feature is "powered by Google Gemini," so it appears it is not considered to be part of Apple Intelligence and thereby extra usage will not be included in iCloud+ plans.

title: Best external SSD for Mac 2026: Top drives tested
content:
Macworld





An external SSD is a straightforward way to expand your Mac’s storage, carry files between devices and keep backups close at hand. Whether you need more room for photos or a fast drive for video projects, our recommendations cover a range of capacities, connections and budgets.
Compared with mechanical hard drives, SSDs generally offer faster transfers in smaller, lighter designs. Most portable models take power directly from your Mac, making them convenient companions for a MacBook. Desktop drives offer another option if your storage will mostly stay in one place.
Choosing the right SSD involves more than finding the highest advertised speed. Your Mac’s ports, the drive’s connection and the supplied cable all affect performance. For everyday backups, capacity and value may matter more than maximum speed; for demanding creative work, faster transfers can justify paying extra.
We compare tested performance, Mac compatibility, portability and value, alongside practical features such as rugged protection, encryption and warranty coverage. Below, you’ll find our top picks for different needs, alternatives worth considering and buying advice to help you choose.

Capacity and value
Password protection through Samsung’s Portable SSD app adds useful security. The rugged casing justifies paying extra if you travel regularly, but the cheaper standard T7 may suffice for desk use.

That’s adequate for Time Machine and mobile photo backups, but modest for demanding editing. Its USB 3.2 Gen 1 interface limits performance even on faster Mac ports. Lexar claims support for direct 4K/60fps ProRes recording. USB-C connectivity works with Macs, but unlocking requires an NFC-equipped phone running the Lexar app.
Design and durability
Measuring 3.35 × 2.09 × 0.28 inches (85 × 53 × 7mm) and weighing 0.09 pounds (40g), the TouchLock is pocketable. A MagSafe-compatible ring holds it against an iPhone. Lexar claims two-meter drop protection, but there’s no IP rating for water or dust resistance. A USB-A adapter is included.
Capacity and value
The TouchLock model we reviewed offers 512GB or 1TB of storage. Its appeal rests on convenient security: NFC unlocking, automatic locking when disconnected and 128-bit encryption. 
Who should buy?
Choose it for straightforward, secure backups when traveling with an iPhone. Consider the Samsung T7 Shield from this roundup for faster transfers and IP65 protection. Mac-only users should weigh the inconvenience of needing a phone to unlock their storage.
Also considered


		
$399.99 at  Seagate (Lacie)										 | 
																$1,850 at  Amazon						
					
The LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5 is a portable Thunderbolt 5 SSD designed for photographers, filmmakers, and other creative professionals. We liked its combination of excellent performance and substantial protection: our testing recorded approximately 5,250MB/s for both reading and writing on a compatible Mac. Its rubberized enclosure carries an IP68 water and dust resistance rating, while a five-year warranty adds reassurance. Available in 2TB and 4TB capacities, it provides ample room for demanding projects without becoming difficult to carry. However, its premium price makes it excessive for ordinary backups, and achieving its best speeds requires Thunderbolt 5. Reports that the model is being discontinued also make availability uncertain. It remains worth considering at a sensible clearance price, but we would prioritize more readily available alternatives.






$119.99 at  Seagate										 | 
																$389.99 at  B&H										 | 
																$684.97 at  Amazon						
					
The LaCie Rugged SSD4 is a portable USB4 drive that combines fast transfers with LaCie’s familiar orange protective sleeve. We liked its strong Mac performance, recording approximately 2,975MB/s for reading and 3,300MB/s for writing – comfortably sufficient for large file transfers and demanding everyday work. Its IP54 rating protects against dust and splashes, while LaCie also specifies resistance to three-meter drops and one-tonne crushing pressure. A three-year warranty with Rescue Data Recovery Services strengthens its appeal for people working away from the office. Our main design complaint was the easily misplaced removable USB port cover. However, reported discontinuation and uncertain stock now undermine its position as a leading recommendation. Consider remaining stock only when the price compares favorably with current USB4 alternatives offering similar performance and protection.






$129.99 at  LaCie						
					





The LaCie Portable SSD is a small USB-C drive aimed at people who want straightforward additional storage without a bulky enclosure. We liked its attractive silver design, solid construction, and exceptionally light, pocketable form. Its USB 3.2 Gen 2 connection offers sufficient performance for everyday transfers, photo libraries, and backups, although it was an average performer within its class rather than a speed leader. Reviewed capacities ranged from 500GB to 2TB, making it suitable for carrying a working collection of documents and media. Its appeal was always the combination of portability, simplicity, and style. However, retailers now identify reviewed models as discontinued or end of life. We would choose a more readily available alternative unless remaining stock comes with a compelling discount and a trustworthy seller.

We liked its strong performance on Macs, with our Thunderbolt 4 MacBook Pro recording approximately 3,400MB/s for both reading and writing. Its forged aluminum body and protective silicone covering give it a reassuringly sturdy feel, supported by IP65 dust and water resistance and a five-year warranty. The main drawback is size: it is noticeably larger and heavier than many portable competitors. SanDisk now offers a newer Extreme Pro V3, so this older model makes more sense as a discounted alternative than the default recommendation. Check the model number carefully: SDSSDE82 identifies this version. 






$94.99 at  Seagate										 |

We liked its light, sturdy construction and the inclusion of both USB-C and USB-A cables, making it convenient to use across different computers. The reviewed model offered 500GB, 1TB, and 2TB capacities, with enough performance for documents, photos, and media libraries. Seagate’s Toolkit software adds folder synchronization. The absence of hardware encryption is a limitation for people carrying sensitive files. It could still be worth buying at a competitive price; be careful to distinguish the faster STKG generation from older STJE models.






$59.99 at  Western Digital										 |

$84.99 at  Lacie										 |

We liked its sturdy construction, pocketable design, and three-year warranty with Rescue Data Recovery Services. It provides a useful way to carry backups or project files when traveling, with reviewed capacities extending to 4TB. However, its USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 interface is a significant consideration for Mac buyers: the Macs used in our testing could not achieve its advertised 2,000MB/s performance. We recorded approximately 900MB/s for writing and 970MB/s for reading, which remains sufficient for routine backups. $209.99 at  Adorama										 | 
																$209.99 at  B&H						
					
The Lexar Armor 700 is a rugged portable SSD aimed at photographers, filmmakers, and anyone carrying important files outdoors. We liked its slim design, grippy protective covering, and IP66 rating for resistance to dust and powerful water jets. Its construction makes it an appealing travel companion, while encryption software provides another useful feature for sensitive files. The important limitation for Mac buyers is its USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 interface: without support for that connection standard, a Mac cannot deliver the drive’s advertised maximum performance. It remains fast enough for ordinary backups, but USB4 alternatives are better suited to buyers prioritizing speed. A substantial discount could still make it an attractive purchase for travel.






$281.06 at  Amazon

We liked its attractive construction, quiet fan, and good transfer speeds. Testing on an M3 MacBook Air produced approximately 2,664MB/s for writing and 3,123MB/s for reading, with stronger results on an M4 Max Mac Studio. Reviewed capacities ranged from 1TB to 4TB. However, sustained testing exposed temporary speed reductions as the drive warmed up, before cooling restored performance. Mac users should also reformat the drive appropriately, and the included software is Windows-only. Other USB4 options offer a clearer combination of performance and convenience. It remains a reasonable alternative when discounted, particularly for everyday transfers that do not involve continuously writing large amounts of data.






The Adata SE920 is a high-performance portable USB4 SSD designed for demanding work such as photo and video editing. We liked its fast, consistent transfers and effective cooling system, which combines a metal enclosure with a small fan. Pressing the housing expands it and activates the fan, giving users additional cooling during sustained activity. The modules are designed to withstand rough handling, and the Station accommodates four of them for a larger storage setup. This makes the system useful for teams exchanging footage or maintaining separate project drives. However, a Mag cannot connect directly to your Mac, so the required enclosure adds cost and complexity. Our Mac testing recorded approximately 943MB/s for writing and 930MB/s for reading, comfortably sufficient for everyday transfers and suitable video recording tasks. Its IP54 rating provides protection against dust and splashes, while Seagate specifies resistance to three-meter drops. However, the short USB-C connector may not reach an iPhone’s port through some protective cases. It remains an appealing alternative for buyers who want compact USB-C storage and value its protective construction.






How we test Mac SSDs
Our reviews combine benchmark results with hands-on use to assess transfer performance, portability, construction and everyday convenience. We identify the test platform where relevant, including results from our colleagues at PCWorld. Performance varies with the computer, connection and workload, so we distinguish measured results from manufacturers’ advertised speeds. We also assess practical details such as cables, power requirements, security features and warranty coverage.
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld has been testing Mac hardware for decades. Our recommendations draw on hands-on reviews from our team and colleagues across Foundry, with particular attention to Mac compatibility, useful performance and value.
How to choose an SSD: Buying advice
You’ve read our recommendations of the best SSDs for Mac owners on the market right now. But how did we reach these decisions, and what general advice should you follow when selecting the best SSD for your needs?
SSDs vs hard drives
Hard drives generally offer more storage for your money, making them a good choice for large backups where capacity matters more than speed. SSDs typically cost more per gigabyte, but provide faster transfers and are usually smaller and lighter. They also have no moving parts, making them better suited to carrying alongside a MacBook.
If you decide in favor of hard drives, see our roundup of the best Mac hard drives.
Which SSD connection should you choose?
For an external SSD, prioritize the connection supported by both the drive and your Mac. A fast SSD can’t deliver its full performance through a slower port or cable. Everyday backups rarely need the fastest connection, while large video projects and frequent transfers can justify paying for USB4 or Thunderbolt.
USB-C doesn’t tell you the speed
USB-C describes the connector’s shape, rather than its transfer speed. Drives with identical-looking USB-C connectors can use different USB or Thunderbolt standards and offer very different performance.
The table below compares connection bandwidth, rather than guaranteed file-transfer speeds.


ConnectionMaximum connection bandwidthBest suited to

USB 3.2 Gen 15GbpsRoutine backups and everyday storage
USB 3.2 Gen 210GbpsGeneral transfers, backups and photo libraries
USB 3.2 Gen 2×220GbpsCompatible computers; limited performance on many Macs
USB4 at 40Gbps / Thunderbolt 3 or 440GbpsLarge transfers and demanding photo or video work
Thunderbolt 580Gbps for storageMaximum performance on compatible Macs

 



USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 deserves particular attention. Macs that support USB transfers at only 10Gbps won’t deliver a Gen 2×2 drive’s advertised 20Gbps performance. A Thunderbolt port doesn’t automatically remove that limitation.
To get the most from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD, you need a Thunderbolt 5-equipped Mac. Its higher storage bandwidth can support much faster transfers, but connecting a slower USB drive to that port won’t increase the drive’s own maximum speed.
What about SATA and NVMe?
SATA and NVMe describe the storage technology inside a drive, rather than the external connection to your Mac. SATA SSDs typically top out at around 550MB/s, while NVMe SSDs use PCIe and can achieve substantially higher speeds.
However, an external enclosure’s connection can become the bottleneck. An NVMe SSD capable of several gigabytes per second internally won’t achieve those speeds through a 10Gbps USB connection.
For a ready-made external SSD, our measured performance is more useful than its internal PCIe generation alone. If you’re assembling your own external drive, choose an enclosure that supports your SSD’s type and a connection your Mac can exploit.
Match the drive, port and cable
Use a cable rated for the drive’s connection standard. If you connect through a hub or dock, its supported speeds and shared bandwidth also matter.
Actual transfers depend on file sizes, sustained-write performance and the storage at the other end. Choose a drive based on its tested performance in the kind of work you do, rather than connection bandwidth alone.
How much SSD storage do you need?
Choosing the right external SSD capacity depends on what you plan to store. Capacities vary by model, with several recommendations here extending to 8TB. Allow enough space for your existing files and room for your collection to grow, especially if you work with photos or video.
These starting points can help:
500GB–1TB: Everyday documents, smaller photo collections and transferring files between devices.
1TB–2TB: Larger photo libraries, individual video projects and more substantial everyday storage.
4TB–8TB: Extensive photo and video collections, multiple large projects or substantial backup archives.
For backups, consider how much data you need to protect and allow additional space for older versions you may want to recover. For a working drive, consider the size of your projects and how many you need to keep available at once. A smaller SSD may suffice if you regularly move completed projects to separate storage.
Avoid buying a drive that your files will fill immediately. Leaving free space provides room to grow and can help maintain performance, although the effect of filling a drive varies by model and workload.
Compare the price per terabyte across capacities. Larger models sometimes offer better value, but the highest capacity isn’t automatically the best deal. Balance the price with the space you’ll realistically use.
How portable does your SSD need to be?
Most external SSDs are small enough to carry in a laptop bag, but size, weight and cable design affect convenience. A compact, lightweight drive suits frequent travel, while built-in connectors eliminate a separate cable but may obstruct an adjacent port.
For outdoor use, look for a sturdy enclosure and a stated IP rating for dust and water resistance. Water resistance doesn’t necessarily mean a drive can withstand immersion.
Also consider power requirements. Most portable SSDs draw power from your Mac, but the SanDisk Desk Drive requires mains power, making it better suited to a permanent desk setup.
Shock-proof and rugged?
Other features to look out for include IP-ratings for weather protection and password protection for your important files.
SSDs are more durable than hard drives. They have no moving parts, and are less vulnerable to knocks and movement than mechanical hard drives while writing data. While modern hard drives have some level of shock protection, it’s still a big issue.
However, SSDs can still suffer physical damage or fail, so handle them carefully and keep another copy of important files.
Some portable SSDs even offer water resistance. You can also get ruggedization in a specialized drive enclosure, if you choose to go down the 2.5in drive route.
This is a huge portability benefit. But if they are sat still all day, are SSDs more reliable than HDDs? Hard drives tend to fail mechanically. For example, the motor that spins the platters might burn out. SSDs’ memory cells age, which can lead to failure. Both kinds require specialist recovery. As ever, 
back up important data.
However, for our purposes, as people who occasionally have to fling drives in rucksacks and plug them in while sat in an airplane seat, SSDs are the clear winner.
Software
Just remember to check that any apps provided by the manufacturer work with Macs as well as Windows PCs.

title: Apple will reportedly eliminate the Action button in 2027
content:
Macworld





Do you use the Action Button? With the iPhone 15 Pro and every model after, Apple replaced the mute switch (an iPhone staple since the original) with a programmable button.
It doesn’t seem to be very popular. Most users seem to just leave it as a Mute toggle, and even then you see people just using the volume buttons to quiet their iPhone.
A new leak from popular Weibo account Instant Digital claims that Apple is going to get rid of it starting with the phones coming in the second half of 2027. Other iPhone models would lose the button over time, as their physical enclosures are updated.
Apple will combine the function of the Action button with the Camera button, according to the leak. You press the Camera button to launch the camera (or press the shutter if you have a camera app/mode open) and you long-press the button to perform the Action button function.
A long-press of the Action button used to invoke Visual Intelligence. When that feature went underutilized, Apple added it as a new “Siri” mode in the Camera app. Now, a long-press on the Camera button opens the Camera app to the Siri mode, which could be confusing as it looks very close to just opening the camera in general. The rumored change would eliminate that issue by taking away the current Camera > Siri default action for holding down the Action button, and replacing it the Mute toggle or other action of your choosing.

title: Apple Pay Ad Features Martial Arts Convenience Store Food Fight
content:
Apple today shared a humorous new Apple Pay ad that promotes the benefit of the on-device payment option over cash and physical cards.



The spot features a martial-arts-style food fight where a man runs into a convenience store to grab a weapon. He's followed by the other combatants, and everyone involved grabs a different food or beverage to fight with.

Face ID verification is required. The protagonist wins when he purchases a swordfish, causing his opponents to flee.
Apple Pay is a fast, easy, and secure way to pay with iPhone. No digging for cards. Just double-click the side button, glance at your iPhone to authenticate with Face ID, then hold it near the reader. A ding confirms your payment. The built-in security of iPhone makes paying with Apple Pay more secure than using a physical credit or debit card. Use it anywhere you see a contactless payment symbol — from big box retailers to your local corner market.

‌Apple Pay‌ is a popular contactless payment option available in many countries around the world. It works in retail shops on iPhone and Apple Watch. ‌Apple Pay‌ also works in apps and on the web, and on iPad and Mac for online purchases.

title: Singapore Saved Apple $2.7 Billion in Taxes This Year
content:
Apple paid more income tax in Ireland than in Singapore in fiscal 2026, but it saved more in Singapore.



annual report shows that the company paid $4.96 billion in cash income taxes in Ireland and $3.25 billion in Singapore. Against the 21% U.S. federal corporate tax rate, Singapore lowered Apple's tax expense by $2.67 billion, about $100 million more than Ireland did.

top-up tax erased nearly half of that initial saving. Singapore introduced the tax to bring the effective tax rate for qualifying large multinationals up to 15%.

new U.S. accounting rules. Apple reported a combined figure for its foreign subsidiaries in fiscal 2025 and 2024, so those years offer no direct comparison between Singapore and Ireland.

Financial Times estimated that Apple booked up to $50 billion in pretax profit in Singapore in 2026. Apple's Singapore subsidiaries reported nearly $40 billion a year earlier.

title: Apple’s new glowing logo on the MacBook Pro has a hidden on-off switch
content:
Macworld





With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. And it’s got a new trick: Turn up the display brightness, and the logo gets brighter, too. Turn down the display brightness, and the logo dims.
However, since the brightness controls on the display and logo are linked, the only way to turn the brightness on the logo all the way down is to also turn off the display. And sadly, Apple did not include a system setting control for the logo, so you can’t turn it off by simply flicking a switch.
But you can turn it off through Terminal, Apple’s command line interface for the Mac. In fact, Apple has a support document with the details.
Turn off the glowing Apple logo
You must be logged into the Mac with an account that has Administrator rights.
Launch Terminal. It is in Applications>Utilities. You can also press Command + Space to bring up Spotlight Search, type “Terminal,” and press Return after “Terminal — Open” appears in the search box.
Copy the following and paste it into Terminal sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0  then press Return
Terminal will ask for your password, which must be a user with Administrator rights. (When typing the password, Terminal will not show the characters.) Press Return and the logo should turn off.
Quit Terminal.
Turn on the glowing Apple logo
Follow the same steps as above, but enter this Terminal command: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode 
The glowing Apple logo is on by default, so if you reinstall macOS after turning it off, it will turn back on.
Or use can use a new app
Fortunately, now, there’s an app for that. Juan Buis created Backglow, a utility that can be used to customize the glowing Apple logo. In addition to turning it off and on, the free version of Backglow provides settings for two different pulse modes and it can remove the brightness limit. If you pay $9 for Backglow Pro, it activates the ability to set the glow pulse to music, and use Claude Code for your own personal pulse modes.

				
					

				
			Backglow can reside in the menu bar for quick access.

title: Some HomePod Mini 2 Buyers Returning Units Over Mac Speaker Issues
content:
One of the features of Apple's new HomePod mini 2 speakers is being able to use them as your Mac's default speakers, but it seems to be failing to work as advertised for a number of users, with some owners already returning them, based on the latest MacRumors forum reports.

OG HomePod minis in a stereo pair on a Mac (don't try this at home)

The new HomePod mini 2 can be used as a default speaker on all Mac models with Wi-Fi 6E or later, according to Apple. A single HomePod can be used alone, or a pair can be twinned for stereo sound. The same setup never reliably worked with the first-generation HomePod mini, with latency and dropout issues common.

HomePod‌ Software 27.2, and it's meant to work over "a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection," or a wireless point-to-point link that's designed to survive restarts and sleep. (That's different to ordinary AirPlay, which the previous-generation HomePod uses.) For the HomePod mini 2, the feature requires macOS 27.2. It's also supposed to work with the second-generation HomePod using the same software and the aforementioned Wi-Fi 6E requirement.

So far, new HomePod mini 2 owners are reporting two separate problems. For some, the option to enable the persistent connection never appears at all – even on hardware that meets Apple's stated requirements. For others, the connection works at first, but the Mac then falls back to its built-in or monitor speakers after sleep, a restart, or sometimes even after a single notification sound.

ran into the first problem in her review for The Verge. On a Mac mini M4 – meeting Apple's Wi-Fi 6E requirement – the persistent-output option never showed up, and the speakers behaved like ordinary AirPlay devices, along with audio artifacts, dropouts, and output switching after a restart or whenever Siri was activated on a HomePod. Tuohy said that the feature "feels unfinished," and Apple had not responded to her request for comment at the time of writing.

MacRumors forum reports. DanJoeWhitaker said they bought a stereo pair solely to use as Mac speakers, but found that the "Play sound effects through" option reverted to their Studio Display speakers within a minute, and that a single notification sound could make their Mac "forget" the HomePods entirely. 

Nismo73, tested a pair on a Mac Studio and was greeted by an error message and sound through the machine's internal speaker after the first wake from sleep. Five owners on the forums describe similar failures, and at least two forum members say they're returning the speakers. DanJoeWhitaker said they were told at an Apple Store that they weren't the first to have the problem – Apple Support's senior team reportedly offered no fix, suggesting the issue was "maybe just an early teething bug."

Redditor with an M3 Max MacBook Pro on a UniFi network. Their Mac's logs showed the point-to-point connection failing while the HomePods were on a 6GHz network, with audio falling back to standard AirPlay at around half a second of latency. Moving the speakers to a 5GHz-only network apparently restored the low-latency persistent mode in that setup. But whether the other failures correlate with 6GHz networks or specific router configurations remains unclear.

Our Verdict 
The SanDisk Extreme Pro delivers fast USB4 performance in a slim, lightweight design, with IP65 protection for life on the move. Its high price and lack of Thunderbolt 5 limit its appeal, but professionals prioritizing portability and durability will still find plenty to like.

What is it? A slim, rugged portable USB4 SSD with fast performance for storing and working with large files. 
Who’s it for? Professionals working with large video and graphics files who need fast, durable storage that’s easy to carry.
Who’s it not for? Budget-conscious buyers or professionals seeking the faster performance available from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD.
SanDisk has updated its entire range of portable solid-state drives, including this third-generation update for the Extreme Pro, which, as the name suggests, is aimed at professional users who need high-end performance when working with large video and graphics files. 
Sadly, like most forms of memory and storage, the Extreme Pro has rocketed in price since our review of the previous version, now starting at $549.99/£489.99 for a model with 2TB storage, or a whopping $1,099.99/£980.99 with 4TB. There’s also an 8TB model planned for next year, although SanDisk hasn’t given any indication of pricing for that model. 
You should also be aware that older versions of the drive are still widely available online, so make sure you select the correct model before buying. Alternatively, you could save some money by buying an older version of the drive – although, of course, it won’t be quite as fast as the latest model.
Design
The Extreme Pro is still an attractive option for professional users looking for a USB4 SSD to use with a Mac, though, with a more compact design than its predecessor, measuring just 110mm long, 58mm wide and 10mm thick, and weighing a mere 65.2g. It’s easy to slip it into a bag or jacket pocket if you’re travelling with your laptop, and there’s a clip for a lanyard (not included) on one corner of the drive to help keep it safe. It boasts a sturdy IP65 rating for weather-resistance, and Sandisk also states that it can survive being dropped from a height of three metres.
Performance
Performance is good too, with Sandisk quoting read and write speeds of 4GB/s and 3.8GB/s, respectively. The drive did fall a little short on read performance in our tests, using the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test, hitting around 3.5GB/s, but it outperformed on write performance, consistently reaching 4.2GB/s. 
The Extreme Pro will certainly be fast enough for pro users working with large video files, although it’s a shame that such an expensive drive is only using a USB4 interface, with no support for the even faster Thunderbolt 5 that is now available on several high-end Mac models.
Should you buy the SanDisk Extreme Pro?
The SanDisk Extreme Pro combines fast USB4 performance with a slim, lightweight design that’s easy to carry alongside your MacBook. Strong write speeds make it appealing for professionals working with large video and graphics files, while IP65 protection and claimed three-meter drop resistance add reassurance when traveling. 
However, read speeds fell short of SanDisk’s claims in our tests, and the lack of Thunderbolt 5 feels disappointing at this price. Starting at $549.99/£489.99 for 2TB, it’s a costly investment. It’s worth considering if portability, durability, and speed are priorities, but the steep price makes it harder to recommend without some reservations.

title: Siri Is Getting a Better Memory
content:
Apple is building a personal memory system that could help Siri retain information about users' lives, based on new code findings shared by code explorer pdfu.


In Apple's iOS 27.3 beta release, the system includes a "memory graph" that's designed to organize information about relationships, places, routines, health, workouts, and what motivates users or holds them back, according to the findings. It also identifies "memory atoms" for facts, opinions, intentions, and events, including details about the people, places, times, and topics involved.

According to pdfu, the graph uses two kinds of processes to gather info. One turns structured data into insights – like reading the name fields in a user's own contact card. The other uses an on-device AI model or Private Cloud Compute to extract insights by querying sources including Siri conversations, messages, photos, and health data.

Apparently, only one of these AI-driven processes is present so far: pdfu believes it's designed to identify motivations, barriers, and resources using a set of 60 built-in questions, including questions about routines that might interfere with adequate sleep.

follow-up explanation, the code sleuth also distinguished the graph from a separate store for explicit memories. The latter store has space for records in Apple's search system, but nothing writes the records yet.

Apple TV 4K: adds Siri AI, the A19 chip, an updated Siri Remote with Find My, and support for four-speaker surround sound with HomePod mini 2. The Apple TV 4K comes with 128GB of storage and is priced at $299.
Both products were announced on October 13 alongside the HomePod mini 2, which launched October 30.

title: Apple Stores ordered to stop signing up unwitting customers to services
content:
Staff at Apple Stores have been pressured into signing up customers to services such as Apple TV, but the practice has reportedly been stopped after it was uncovered.


No specific Apple Stores have been identified over this subscription practice, but reportedly all stores have been directed to stop. This is Tysons Corner Apple Store in 2023.
Apple has previously cracked down on other firms pushing subscriptions on unwitting users, but now it has been doing something similar. Whether Apple expressly sanctioned it or just created the pressure on its employees, staff at Apple Stores have reportedly been signing up users to free trials without telling them.
The practice was uncovered by Louis Rossmann, previously best known as a critic of Apple's repair policies. In the latest of a series of YouTube videos, he has explained how the practice worked.

title: 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display review: Simply irresistible
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Amazing tandem OLED display
Excellent performance
Smaller and lighter
Touch input
Cons
Some Touch UI quirks
Our Verdict 
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display raises the bar of Apple excellence. It’s a landmark addition to the Mac lineup, and it’s a reminder of what makes users devoted to the Mac. It’s a good time to be a Mac user.
Price When Reviewed

With its newest MacBook, Apple takes the idea of a Pro laptop to another level. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the most expensive model in the lineup. It’s made to appeal to the most demanding professionals, especially those who take content creation seriously and are willing to pay a premium.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t for everyone, but even if you don’t fit into its intended audience, you will want this laptop. All it takes is one look. It is glorious, it is profound, and it is effing awesome–pardon my thinly-veiled language, but that’s just how I feel about this laptop. This, dear reader, is Apple’s finest MacBook to date and probably the best laptop ever made.
Our model’s specifications
This review looks at a model that’s been customized from Apple’s standard offerings. It has some hefty add-ons that increase the price significantly. Here are the specifications of the laptop in this review:
CPU: M5 Max with an 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores); 16-core Neural Engine
GPU: 40 cores
Memory: 128GB unified memory
Storage: 2TB SSD
Display: 16.3-inch tandem OLED; 3472-by-2266 native resolution at 254 pixels per inch; 1000 nits sustained XDR brightness, 2000 nits peak (HDR content only); 1000 nits SDR brightness, 2000 nits peak (outdoor); 1 billion colors; P3 + Adobe RGB wide color gamut; True Tone; standard glass
Ports: 3 Thunderbolt 5/USB-C; MagSafe 3; SDXC Card slot; HDMI; 3.5mm audio
Networking: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be); Bluetooth 6; Thread
Input devices: Touchscreen; Magic Keyboard with Touch ID; Magic Trackpad
Weight: 4.1 pounds (1.84 kg)
Dimensions: 0.63 x 14.0 x 9.62 inches (1.60 x 35.55 x 24.42 cm)
Price (as tested): $7,399/£7,399

				
					

				
			
The touchscreen MacBook Pro’s OLED display offers new highs in brightness and great color fidelity

Roman Loyola/Foundry




PROLED MacBook Pro: Display
As the name implies, the tandem OLED display is the key feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. This is the main reason to spend the extra $400 over the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED backlit display.
When I unpacked the laptop, opened it for the first time, and the display lit up, I instantly knew I was in for a special experience. The brightness of the tandem OLED makes an immediate impression. With the right wallpaper, such as the macOS Golden Gate default photo, the brightness gives the image an aura that feels magical.
It’s an admirable feat to outdo the mini-LED backlit displays that Apple replaced, because they’re excellent displays in their own right. The tandem OLED is more than up to the task. Color saturation and evenness are more pleasing, and the contrast and blacks are deeper. At the Macworld office, my desk is set up with a first-generation Apple Studio Display and a Dell UltraSharp 32 4K QD-OLED Monitor U3226Q, which is made for production work. Yet I prefer looking at the PROLED XDR Display. You will want to work on photos, video, and graphics on this MacBook Pro.
If that work takes you outside, well, don’t worry. I’m currently writing this display section of the review in my backyard, because it’s a perfect San Francisco day, a bright and sunny 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20°C). It’s early afternoon, and the sun is bearing down directly on the display and me. Yet the screen shines through like a champ. Glare and reflections? No problem, thanks to the OLED’s brightness working with the antireflective coating on the glass. Don’t hesitate to go outside or take this MacBook Pro on location. I’d actually stay outside longer if it wasn’t for the fact that the sun is starting to cook me, which makes me a little concerned about the laptop heating up, too.

				
					

				
			
MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display with standard glass (left) is much more visbile in direct sunlight than the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED backlit Nano-texture glass display (right).

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Since this is the first time OLED is on the Mac, you might be concerned about burn-in–if you’re going to spend the extra $400, it better last. Only time will tell with the new MacBook Pro, but Apple updated the display engine for OLED, and it monitors the OLED’s condition to maintain optimal performance and minimize the burn-in risk. Apple uses OLED displays in its iPhones, and it introduced a tandem OLED in the iPad Pro in 2024. We haven’t heard of widespread burn-in problems with those devices.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Touch UI
There’s been a lot of anticipation about this being Apple’s first touchscreen Mac. Touchscreen Windows laptops have long been available, and Apple has repeatedly said that touchscreen input on the Mac wasn’t going to happen. Times change. Generations of people have grown up with touch interfaces, and the lack of touch on the Mac is something that prevented some from switching from Windows. There’s a demand for touch.

				
					

				
			Touch on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is responsive, and macOS’s main elements have been adjusted to accommodate fingers.
Roman Loyola/Foundry




I wrote a separate article that details the Touch experience, but here’s the TL;DR version. Apple’s Touch implementation is so good, it can replace the trackpad as your regular input device. Apple didn’t half-ass it here. The company made thoughtful decisions about how the interface should respond to touch, and the result is responsive and reliable. There are a few quirks, but nothing that stops you in your tracks, and you can always retreat to the trackpad.
Touch worked with all the Apple apps and third-party software I tried, but it didn’t work on some games. For example, Resident Evil Village and Total War: Warhammer III do not let you use Touch, and I suspect this is the case for a lot of games that originated on Windows and implement their own maps for input. You probably wouldn’t want to use Touch during gameplay, but it would be convenient when starting a game and navigating its setup screens and settings. Unfortunately, Touch doesn’t work in those situations, either.

				
					

				
			
The touchscreen supports Multi-Touch gestures, which can be modified in a new Touch Display section of System Settings.

Apple




While Apple has done a good job with its first Touch implementation, it’s not a spotlight feature–Touch isn’t even in the name of this new MacBook. I’d go so far as to say that the laptop just happens to have Touch. Apple hasn’t done anything here that requires Touch, so you can buy it, never use Touch, and you won’t miss out on anything. But if Touch is the main reason why you’re considering this laptop, you’ll find it a satisfying implementation, and Apple has gone on record saying it is committed to its development.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Design
Apple took this opportunity to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lighter and a little smaller. Below is a comparison of the dimensions for the 16-inch MacBook Pro models in Apple’s current lineup.


Dimension16″ MacBook Pro
with PROLED XDR Display
M5 Max16″ MacBook Pro
M5 Max

Height0.63 in (1.60 cm)0.66 in (1.68 cm)
Width14.0 in (35.55 cm)14.01 in (35.57 cm)
Depth9.62 in (24.42 cm)9.77 in (24.81 cm)
Weight4.1 lb (1.86 kg)4.7 lb (2.15 kg)

 



The size difference between the two laptops is inconsequential overall. The feet are slightly recessed as well, so it rests closer to the table and a smidge lower than the standard model, so you’ll get a bit more wiggle room in tight spaces. 

				
					

				
			
The mini-LED backlit MacBook Pro with an aluminum logo is a bit taller than the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




On the other hand, the weight difference is huge. The PROLED XDR Display laptop is 12 percent lighter than the standard MacBook Pro, and that’s noticeable when carrying it around on a bus commute. The laptop’s shell retains the same general design as before, in the same two colors Space Black and Silver. However, the corners of the display are a bit more rounded than before and now the bottom of the display is rounded as well. Also the hinge has been adjusted to better accommodate taps and swipes.
However, since you’ll want people to know you’re using one of these laptops, Apple added a bit of flourish to the back by replacing the shiny aluminum Apple logo with one that glows. It’s a callback to the era when the Mac laptops had the glowing Apple logo from 1999 to 2015. No other MacBook has it, and with its placement on Apple’s most expensive and extravagant laptop, the glowing Apple is now a status symbol. 
As with the older implementations, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen’s brightness. Turn up the screen, and the logo brightens; turn down the screen, and the logo dims. If you want to turn it off completely, you need to use a Terminal command, as detailed in an Apple support document–odd that it’s not an option in System Settings.

				
					

				
			
The glowing Apple logo on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (right) used to be on older laptops, such as the 2010 MacBook Pro (left).

Roman Loyola/Foundry




PROLED MacBook Pro: Dynamic Island
Did you hate the notch at the top of Apple’s MacBook displays? It’s gone! Rejoice! But it’s not forgotten, because there’s still a camera hole at the top of the display. Apple opted to cut an opening for the FaceTime camera rather than place it under the display as it does with the iPhone Duo‘s inside display. Considering how poor we found the Duo camera’s image quality is, sticking with a cutout (and a smaller one at that) is the right choice. One small side effect: The new camera cutout is slightly lower than the notch was, so it means the menu bar is a little deeper.
Instead of simply replacing the notch with a static pill-shaped cutout, Apple has brought the Dynamic Island to macOS, displaying notifications, Spotlight search, Siri AI, Live Activities, and more. It works as it does on the iPhone. I’m glad it’s on the Mac, but it did take some adjustment, because these elements are now at the top center of the display, whereas before they either popped up in the middle of the display or off to the right. 

				
					

				
			
The notch is gone on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. A less distracting, iPhone-like pillbox replaces it.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




An important thing to know is that Live Activities isn’t a feature that’s only for Dynamic Island. In the macOS 27.3 beta, the feature works on other Macs, appearing as a small oval in the menu bar. But it’s much more elegant here.
The FaceTime camera has CenterStage, like the standard MacBook Pro. But it also has advanced video stabilization, which you won’t find on any other MacBook. I’m not sure how crucial this feature is, since I don’t typically move my laptop around while using the camera. But since this laptop is targeted at content creation, it’s a feature Apple felt was necessary.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Performance
New laptop, new chip, right? Nope. Apple is using the M5 Pro or M5 Max for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the same chips that were released in the MacBook Pro earlier this year. This decision stems from changes to Apple’s chip development plans in response to growing demand for AI processing. However, the chip series Apple decided to fast-track, the M7, isn’t ready, so M5 chips it is.
The M5 Max is impressive, and fortunately, the major new component of the laptop, the OLED, doesn’t affect chip performance. So, across the board, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and the standard model offer the same speed.

		
			


If you want the fastest MacBook Pro, it’s the one with the M5 Max chip and the 40-core GPU, tested here. The M5 Max is 26 percent faster than the M4 Max and 45 percent faster than the M3 Max in Geekbench’s Multi-Core CPU benchmark. Geekbench checks the overall CPU performance.

		
			


Cinebench is a benchmark tool that uses Maxon’s Redshift render engine, so it’s a good gauge for professionals who handle content. The M5 Max is 18 percent faster than the M4 Max, and 38 percent faster than an M3 Max.

		
			


The difference between the M5 Max and M4 Max here isn’t noticeable. They both rely on the built-in encoder on each chip, and Apple didn’t make many changes between the two chips.

		
			


A 4K iMovie video export at the High setting was 14 percent faster on the M5 Max than on the M4 Max. With the export set to Best (ProRes), there’s no difference.

		
			


Apple introduced major SSD speed improvements with the MacBook Pro earlier this year, and they’re in this new laptop, too. Interestingly, the PROLED laptop’s read speed is noticeably faster than what we’ve seen previously.

		
			


You know what looks really nice? Video games on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. While there are gaming PC laptops, Apple’s new laptop doesn’t really compete with them, since those devices optimize for video performance. Apple’s laptop performs well, but Windows has a distinct advantage when it comes to the available game library.

		
			

		
		

		
			


The M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display mirrors the results of the M5 Max Mac Studio in Geekbench’s AI tests. If you’re an AI developer, it’s nice to know that you won’t lose performance while using a laptop.
PROLED MacBook Pro: Battery life
The 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has the same 99.6-watt-hour battery as its mini-LED backlit companion. Thus, both laptops with the M5 Max chip have the same rating of 22 hours of video streaming and 16 hours of wireless web use.
Our test for battery life involves saving a video to the SSD and then running it on a continuous loop until the battery runs out. With the display set to 150 nits, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lasted about 24 hours, the same as the 15-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with mini-LED.

				
					

				
			
Apple has not changed the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s ports. Pictured here: MagSafe, two Thunderbolt 5/USB ports, audio jack.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Apple has not commented on whether OLED uses more power than mini-LED. Since OLED technology switches off to display black, it could conceivably use less power, since the backlight with mini-LED is always on, even with black. On the other hand, OLED gets much brighter than mini-LED, so it can use more power in high-brightness situations. With this in mind, macOS’s dark mode could help this laptop save energy (plus it looks great).
The same stuff
In addition to the chip options, there is a lot more about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display that’s the same as the standard MacBook Pro. Here’s a quick summary of the features that are the same.
Ports: three Thunderbolt 5/USB 4 ports, an HDMI port, a MagSafe connector, an SDXC Card slot, and a 3.5mm audio jack. If you want more details on the ports, you can read our M4 Pro MacBook Pro review.
External displays: With the M5 Max, the PROLED MacBook Pro supports up to four displays at native resolutions of 6K at 60Hz or 4K at 144Hz. It can also display two screens at up to a native resolution of 8K at 60Hz, 5K at 120Hz, or 4K at 240Hz.
Wireless connectivity: Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be), Bluetooth 6, and Thread.
Speakers: six-speaker sound system with force-canceling woofers.
Backlit Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and Magic Trackpad.

				
					

				
			
An SDXC Card slot, Thunderbolt 5/USB, and HDMI.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Should you buy the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display?
Gawd, I love the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. I’m excited every time I use it. The OLED display is a revelation. Touch is intriguing and sometimes fun. The performance is satisfying. The lighter weight and smaller design are a welcome relief. The pill-shaped camera cutout is much less of a visual detraction than the notch, and the Dynamic Island is useful. It’s a laptop that gets everything right.
If you can afford it, I recommend the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display to anyone. No matter what kind of work you do, you should use the best tools available, right? That’s this MacBook. The reality, however, is that everything is more expensive than it’s ever been. We all need to take a deeper consideration of costs, so here’s more specific advice.
If you are a professional whose work depends on visual integrity, this laptop is a vital tool. The OLED display will help you excel at what you do. It’s worth the investment, and you’ll find it will pay for itself in no time.
For other professionals whose work isn’t graphically dependent, the M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro with the mini-LED backlit display is more than capable of meeting your needs. The display has always been great and doesn’t disappoint. It offers the same chip performance as the PROLED model, the same external display support, the same ports, and the same speakers. If you don’t need or really want the OLED display, there’s no need to pay for it. But you’ll still be happy that you did.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display raises the bar for Apple excellence. It’s a landmark addition to the Mac lineup, and a reminder of what makes users devoted to the Mac. Customers now have plenty of laptop choices, with the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It’s a good time to be a Mac user.

title: Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger review: An Apple charging station with room for iPad
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating

Fast Watch Charger
60W USB-C port
Cons

Our Verdict 
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is a tidy charging stand that will clear your desk from straggling cables, wirelessly for the iPhone, Watch, and AirPods, plus an iPad or even MacBook via a wired connection. You can buy cheaper and faster charging stands, but the neat iPad support helps this one stand out. Just remember that the USB-C output drops to 18W when wireless charging is also in use.

What is it? A charging stand that wirelessly charges iPhone, AirPods and Apple Watch, and hosts a charging port for an iPad or MacBook.
Who is it best for? iPad users who want to charge all their Apple devices at the same time.
Who should skip it? If you don’t have an iPad, you’ll be better off with a 3-in-1 or even 2-in-1 (if you don’t have an Apple Watch) wireless charger.
There are many 2-in-1 wireless charging stands (iPhone and AirPods) and 3-in-1 (iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch) magnetic multi marvels, and we’ve tested a large selection of them in our best wireless iPhone charger roundup.
If you want to charge your iPad at the same time as all the above Apple devices, you’ll generally need a second cable from the wall or even two chargers.
3-in-1 magnetic wireless chargers can hoist even the iPhone Pro Max aloft but most would buckle and fall over if you introduced even an iPad mini into the action. The iPad requires a different charging connection, so we’ll stop a moment to explain the options.
How do you wirelessly charge an iPad?
As it doesn’t come with built-in MagSafe charging coils, you can’t simply place an iPad on wireless chargers like you do with an iPhone. The closest you’ll get is the Kuxiu M30 magnetic smart connector charger that brings a MagSafe-like charging experience to compatible iPads by snapping magnetically to the back of the tablet and drawing power through a 3-pogo-pin Smart Connector. Because iPads with these pins have them in different configurations, you need a size-specific charger for select iPad Pro and iPad Air models—it’s a neat solution but nowhere near as convenient as MagSafe/Qi2.
There are several reasons why iPads don’t do MagSafe. iPads have larger batteries than iPhones (19-40Wh vs 12-20Wh), and these generate too much heat to be safe if charged wirelessly. Also, most iPads use aluminum on their back shells compared to iPhone’s glass, and this interferes with the magnetic fields used in wireless charging.

				
					

				
			The Zens 4-in-1 is a neat stand with charging points for iPhone (raised and ready for StandBy Mode), Apple Watch (supporting Nightstand Mode), AirPods (on the other side to the Watch charger), and a bar to rest your iPad when charging via the side USB-C port.
Simon Jary




Zens offers a simple 4-in-1 solution
The Zens 4-1 Wireless Charger looks like a standard sleek 3-in-1 iPhone charging stand made from zinc alloy but has a bar at the back to prop up an iPad, with a powerful USB-C port on one side to connect it.
It’s a good-looking stand, with Apple’s badge of approval as it is one of few available at the Apple Store.
At the front there’s an elevated iPhone charging pad that’s tilt-adjustable up and down, but not side to side. This is a Qi2 charger and so maxes power output to the iPhone at 15W rather than the latest and greatest 25W Qi2.2. The difference is about 15 minutes (45 vs 30 minutes) in the time it takes to wirelessly charge an iPhone from 0-50%. Compatible newer iPhones can charge faster with a suitable higher-powered wireless charger, but if you charge your devices overnight, the Zens stand’s 15W limit shouldn’t bother you.

				
					

				
			You can flatten the Watch charger when not in use.
Simon Jary




The pop-up Apple Watch module on the Zens 4-1 Wireless Charger can be charged at a rapid 7.5W, faster than most 5W Watch chargers that are able to claim Apple’s official “Fast Charge” status. The AirPods charge at up to 5W, which is as much power as they can take on board, so you won’t get faster.

				
					

				
			The Zens 4-in-1 ships with a 12-inch cable to connect the iPad. It will serve a MacBook too, but you can’t squeeze the laptop into the same space as the iPad slips into.
Simon Jary




At the side is the USB-C port for attaching your iPad, or a second iPhone or any USB-C charged device via the included 12-inch (300mm) cable. It’s rated at up to 60W when used alone, which is enough to charge an iPad or a compatible MacBook. Indeed, it’s enough to fast-charge an iPad—if you’re not charging anything else at the same time. Everyone’s in a hurry sometimes, and if you want to power-up your iPhone as fast as possible use the port and cable for faster wired charging when the wireless charging modules aren’t in use. You’ll need a Lightning cable if your phone is older than an iPhone 15. If you want to connect your MacBook further away, look for a longer USB-C cable.
The Zens 4-in-1 ships with a 65W wall charger (and 5ft/1.5m cable), so you’ll need to share that amount of power around the devices when charging several at the same time. It’s not a USB-C wall charger so is proprietary to the Zens charger.
Note that, as with most multi-device chargers, power output is reduced when charging several devices simultaneously. The USB-C port’s maximum output drops from 60W to 18W when wireless charging is also in use—enough to charge an iPad, although more slowly than when the port is used alone. For a MacBook, whether it can maintain the battery level will depend on the model and workload.
Handily, the Zens 4-in-1 also comes with interchangeable plugs for US (Type A), UK (Type G), and EU (Type C). That doesn’t make it a convenient travel charger, mind you—it’s relatively compact at 6.9 x 5.9 x 4.3 inches (175 x 150 x 110mm) but not one you’ll likely slip into your backpack. It also weighs 23 oz (650g). In comparison, the more travel-friendly Mous 3-In-1 Wireless Portable Charger weighs 85g, although it’s painfully slow at 7.5W.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




How much does the Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger cost?
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is priced at $159.99 / £159.99, although you’ll find it a little cheaper on the Apple Store ($149.95 / £149.95) and maybe Amazon depending on your timing.
You can certainly buy cheaper charging stations but few with the ability to charge a fourth device at the same time. One alternative is Mophie’s 4-in-1 StealthCharge Wireless Charge Stand ($179.95 / £139.95), which has a smaller footprint and 25W iPhone charging—although while it can charge a fourth device via its integrated retractable cable, it lacks the Zens charger’s neat iPad stand bar.
Should you buy the Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger?
The Zens 4-in-1 Wireless Charger is a tidy white/silver charging stand that will reduce cable clutter on your desk for up to four of your devices, wirelessly for the iPhone, Watch and AirPods, plus an iPad or even MacBook via a wired connection. You can buy cheaper and faster charging stands, but the neat iPad support helps this one stand out. Just remember that the USB-C output drops to 18W when wireless charging is also in use.
