title: Pro-privacy Apple could end up as a Trojan Horse for surveillance tech
content:
Macworld





Two of the things I dislike most about modern life are AI and surveillance. So naturally, I was pretty jazzed in September when Apple announced Siri Recap and Live Rewind, two new AI-powered surveillance features coming to the Apple Watch Series 12. Ain’t that just a kick in the head, I thought.
But I was wrong. Or, at least, overreacting a little. As sinister listening technologies go, the Audio Intelligence features are pretty harmless.
Live Rewind, for example, has very clearly been designed from the ground up with privacy in mind, to the extent that its usefulness is frequently limited by such considerations. The tiny 15-second listening window, the limited physical range, the lack of speaker attribution, the inability to screenshot transcripts: all mildly annoying for good-faith users, and devastating for bad actors and eavesdroppers. Yes, these features listen in on you and the people around you. But they do so in the most privacy-friendly way you can imagine.
Apple has long marketed itself as the pro-privacy tech company, but the privacy measures in Audio Intelligence are hardcore even by its standards. (Live Rewind would be a lot more useful if its maker embraced the creepy tech vibe. I’m not saying Apple should have done that; I’m just pointing it out.) And there’s a good reason for Apple’s overabundance of caution: as a general rule, normal people despise listening tech, and the company doesn’t want that kind of controversy.
We’ve been here before, you see. Any technology that’s perceived as listening in on us without informed consent is liable to stir up a passionate response.
Take Google Glass. Google launched its range of smart glasses back in 2012, and their ability to semi-covertly record audio and video of passers-by made them so unpopular that wearers were called “Glassholes” and, in a few cases, were physically assaulted. Then in 2013 the launch of the Xbox One was overshadowed by privacy concerns after it emerged that the device’s Kinect peripheral could monitor users’ conversations; Microsoft was obliged to reverse a previously announced policy that the Kinect had to be plugged in at all times.
Paranoid or not, many tech users suspect that the digital voice assistants in our phones and smart speakers record what we say at all times, despite makers’ insistence that this only happens when the trigger phrase is uttered. Fairly obviously, some form of listening is necessary for the trigger phrase to be recognised, but the theory is that any other audio that’s heard is promptly discarded. Except when it’s not. “I felt invaded,” said one Alexa user whose private conversation was recorded and sent to a random number in her address book. “A total privacy invasion.”
Perhaps we’d expect that kind of thing from Amazon, whose business model relies on extensive data about potential customers. But even Apple has been caught with its hand in the data jar. A class-action lawsuit filed in 2019 alleged that Siri had listened in on users’ conversations and then shared the results with advertisers. Apple denied any wrongdoing but last year settled for $95m.
Considering public distrust of surveillance technology and anger against private individuals who enable it, we can hardly be surprised that Apple is treading so lightly in the execution of its Audio Intelligence features. It doesn’t want to be perceived as spying on its users, and it doesn’t want Apple Watch owners to be attacked. (I don’t want that either, to be clear.) The privacy measures in Audio Intelligence are as thoughtful as they are predictable, and I think they will be accepted in good faith.
But here’s my worry. Apple is very good at leading cultural shifts, either through marketing clout or its ability to absorb the hits and keep fighting. It dropped the headphone port from the iPhone in 2016, a time when such a move seemed unthinkable. Everyone complained, then it became the new normal and other companies followed suit. Apple performed a similar trick by removing the bundled earbuds and charger from iPhone boxes in 2020, which too became accepted in time. It kickstarted the popularity of MP3 players, smartphones, tablets, smartwatches, and wireless earbuds simply by entering those markets, and the launch of the iPhone Duo is widely expected to send foldables into the mainstream.
So what happens if Apple does something similar with eavesdropping tech? Can the company launder the reputation of this singularly hated branch of technology? Can it get people to accept the idea that the things they say are constantly being recorded and fed into AI models?
Other companies will be watching the progress of Live Rewind and Siri Recap with great interest. The execution of these features strikes me as intentional, considered, and ethical. But the fundamental idea is still an unpalatable one: They listen in without explicit consent, and they record in some way what they hear. That remains, for the time being, an idea that would struggle to gain mainstream acceptance. 
But Apple may be about to help it achieve that. And that’s when it becomes a lot easier for other applications to build a user base. Applications that care a lot less about privacy, and a lot more about grabbing data. Ain’t that just a kick in the head.

				
					

				
			
Foundry

title: macOS versions in order: Complete Mac OS X and macOS history
content:
Macworld





Since the debut of Mac OS X in 2001, Apple has released dozens of versions of its Mac operating system, introducing new features, design updates, performance improvements, and more. From early big-cat releases such as Panther and Leopard to more recent California-inspired versions like Sonoma, Sequoia, Tahoe and Golden Gate, each release marked a new chapter in the Mac’s evolution.
Whether you’re trying to identify the version running on your Mac, check compatibility before upgrading, or find out which releases are still supported, this guide covers every Mac OS X and macOS version in chronological order – from the original Mac OS X Cheetah to macOS 27 Golden Gate. 
Discover the major features introduced with each release, including Spotlight in Tiger, Time Machine in Leopard, Siri in Sierra and the enhanced Spotlight search introduced in macOS 27 Golden Gate.
Below, you’ll find a complete list of macOS versions in order, along with release dates, codenames, key details and support information.


What is the latest macOS version? 
macOS 27 Golden Gate was released on September 14, 2026, but the latest version is macOS 27.2, which was released on October 26, 2026 and improved Siri’s memory and use of personal context, added conversation-based suggestions in Messages and enhanced Shared Albums, alongside bug fixes and security updates. 
Apple will continue to update Golden Gate with new features throughout 2026 and 2027.
For details of the latest macOS 27 release, new features, beta updates and compatibility, see our complete macOS 27 Golden Gate Guide.






macOS version history: Every macOS and Mac OS X version and the features it brought 
macOS is Apple’s operating system for the Mac, in the same way iOS runs on the iPhone and iPadOS runs on the iPad. It provides the user interface and acts as the link between a Mac’s hardware and its software.
All Macs have run macOS – formerly known as Mac OS X – since its debut in 2001. Before that, Apple computers used Mac OS 9. macOS is based on Unix technology developed at NeXT, the company Steve Jobs founded before returning to Apple.
Since its launch on March 24, 2001, macOS has evolved significantly, gaining tighter integration with iOS devices, cloud services, and productivity features such as Time Machine, Quick Look, Exposé, Spaces, and Desktop Stacks.
Below is a complete overview of macOS versions, showing how Apple’s desktop operating system has developed over time, along with the official names and internal codenames used for each release.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




OS X 10 beta: Released in September 13, 2000, this preview version of OS X was codenamed Kodiak. It was based on technology from NeXT Computer, which was another company founded by Apple founder Steve Jobs and it introduced the Aqua user interface as well as protected memory and preemptive multitasking to stop crashes. This beta cost $29.95.
OS X 10.0: Code named Cheetah, this was the first major release of Mac OS X, arriving on March 14, 2001. It was Apple’s first OS built on a Unix-based foundation. Unfortunately it was slow and rough around the edges.
OS X 10.1: Just a few months ofter the first version of Mac OS X launched, Apple introduced the Puma update on September 15, 2001. This time is was stable and ready for everyday use, hardware support was better, and other issues with the fist version were addressed. 
OS X 10.2: Jaguar arrived on August 14, 2002, significantly improving performance and usability, introducing Quartz Extreme for smoother graphics, a faster Finder, and better networking. iChat was one of the new features. 
OS X 10.3: In October 2003 Apple introduced Panther which focused on speed, stability, and polish, delivering noticeably faster performance and a more responsive system. New features included: Exposé for managing windows, Fast User Switching, and FileVault disk encryption. Safari arrived as the default web browser.
OS X 10.4: Tiger arrived in April 2005 with new features like Spotlight search and Dashboard widgets. 
OS X 10.5: In October 2007 Leopard arrived and added features like Time Machine for automated backups, Spaces for virtual desktops, and a redesigned Finder with Cover Flow. Time Machine also arrived as a simple way to back up a Mac. 
OS X 10.6: Released in 2009, Snow Leopard focused on performance, stability, and efficiency rather than flashy new features.
OS X 10.7 Lion: Arriving in July 2011, Lion brought iPad-inspired features to the Mac, like Launchpad, full-screen apps, and multi-touch gestures. It also introduced system-wide Auto Save, Resume, and Versions so that users didn’t need to worry about manual saving. 
OS X 10.8: A year later, in 2012 Mountain Lion brought more iOS features to the Mac including Messages, Reminders, Notes, Notification Center, and iCloud integration. Gatekeeper security was also emphasised. 

				
					

				
			The Notification Center made its debut in OS X Mavericks.
Foundry




OS X 10.9: In October 2013 Apple stopped naming Mac OS X versions after big cats and switched to Californian landmarks, starting with Mavericks. It introduced features like Finder Tabs, Tags, and memory compression, making Macs faster and more responsive. It was also the first time Apple offered the Max OS X update for free. 
OS X 10.10: Introduced in October 2014, Yosemite brought a major visual redesign with a cleaner, flatter interface, translucent elements, and a more modern look inspired by iOS (iOS 7 with its big redesign had been introduced in 2013). Continuity features from the iPhone and iPad included Handoff, iCloud Drive, and the ability to make and receive calls and texts from a Mac. 
OS X 10.11: El Capitan arrived in September 2015 and, like Snow Leopard in 2007, focused more on refinement and stability. It brought improvements like better window management (Split View), smoother graphics, and performance boosts.
macOS 10.12: In September 2016 macOS Sierra was the first version to be referred to as macOS rather than Mac OS X, better aligning it with iOS, watchOS and tvOS. It brought Siri to the Mac and improved integration with iPhone and iPad with features like Universal Clipboard. 
macOS 10.13: This was another update where the focus was on performance rather than flashy new features. High Sierra in September 2017 brought updates to core apps like Photos and Safari but mostly focused on security and efficiency updates.
macOS 10.14: In September 2018, Mojave introduced a system-wide Dark Mode and introduced Desktop Stacks for better file organization. 

				
					

				
			Dark Mode debuted in Mojave.
Foundry




macOS 10.15: Arriving in October 2019, Catalina replaced iTunes with separate Music, TV, and Podcasts apps and introduced Sidecar so an iPad could be used as a second display for a Mac. It also ended support for 32-bit apps.
macOS 11: Big Sur was the first version to drop the ten, from Mac OS X, and start again at 11. Launched in November 2020 it was a major redesign of Apple’s Mac operating system, with a cleaner, more modern interface, updated icons, a refined Control Center, and closer visual alignment with iOS.
macOS 12: Arriving in October 2021, Monterey introduced Universal Control (one mouse/keyboard across Mac and iPad) and improved FaceTime.
macOS 13: macOS Ventura arrived in October 2022 and introduced Stage Manager for better multitasking, improved Continuity features (including using an iPhone as a webcam, and brought major updates to Mail, Safari, and Spotlight. Read: How Ventura and Monterey compare. 
macOS 14: In September 2023 Sonoma made the desktop more immersive with animated wallpapers and desktop widgets you can interact with. There were game-focused improvements in Game Mode and video conferencing features like Presenter Overlay were added. Here’s how Sonoma compares to Ventura. 
macOS 15: A year later in September 2024, Sequoia brought iPhone Mirroring and added Apple Intelligence features. Here’s how Sequoia compares to Sonoma. 
macOS 26: Tahoe arrived in September 2025 with a bold new Liquid Glass design with transparent, customizable interface elements and tighter integration with iPhone and iPad. As with iPhone and iPad, Apple unified version numbering, so the macOS jumped from macOS 15 to 26. Apple also expanded Apple Intelligence, improved Spotlight, improved the Phone related features, and added a new Games app. This was the final macOS version to support Intel-based Macs. See how macOS 26 Tahoe compares to macOS 15 Sequoia.
macOS 27: macOS 27 Golden Gate was released on September 14, 2026, bringing Siri AI, Visual Intelligence, enhanced Spotlight search, performance improvements, and refinements to the Liquid Glass interface introduced with macOS Tahoe. Golden Gate is also the first major macOS release to require Apple silicon, ending support for Intel-powered Macs. See how macOS 27 Golden Gate compares to macOS 26 Tahoe.





List of macOS versions and latest versions
Here’s an overview of every version of macOS and Mac OS X Apple has released. You’ll find a complete list of each version of OS X and macOS, along version code names, internal code names (if available) and the most recent version and when it was released. 

				
					

				
			macOS Tahoe.

 FAQ 


1.
Which macOS versions are still supported?
macOS 27 Golden Gate: The current version, receiving new features, bug fixes and security updates.
macOS 26 Tahoe: The previous major version, continuing to receive security updates.
macOS 15 Sequoia: Also continuing to receive security updates.
Apple released macOS 27.2, macOS 26.7.2 and macOS 15.8.2 on October 26, 2026.
Apple generally issues security updates for the current macOS release and the previous two major versions, but this pattern should not be treated as a guaranteed support period.
macOS Sonoma appears to have left the regular update cycle; its most recent update was macOS 14.8.9 on August 6, 2026. Older versions can occasionally receive exceptional fixes, but those releases do not indicate ongoing regular support.
See: How long do Macs and MacBooks last? We also have a full list of which Macs run which versions of macOS here.





2.
How does Apple choose Mac OS X and macOS names?
As you can see from the list above, with the exception of the first OS X beta, all versions of the Mac operating system from 2001 to 2012 were named after big cats, from Cheetah to Panther to the final release, Mountain Lion. But while the public-facing builds were named after big cats, internally, they were named after wines (aside from OS X 10.6 which had no codename).
Even after Apple switched public-facing code names to places in California back in 2013, it carried on naming them after wines internally until 2014. In 2015, Apple decided to change the theme of internal code names from wines to types of apples. 
In 2016, Apple took the plunge to unify the branding of its operating systems by rebranding Mac OS X to macOS, which sits nicely alongside iOS, tvOS, and watchOS and paved the way for macOS 11, the successor to Mac OS X, which arrived twenty years after the first beta of Mac OS X.
In 2025, Apple decided to sync up the numbering system between all its operating systems, moving from macOS 14 to macOS 26 to better reflect the year. macOS 26 Tahoe lived most its lifetime as the most recent version in the year 2026 before being replaced with macOS 27 in September 2026.





3.
How do I check my macOS version?
You can tell which version of macOS you are running by clicking on the Apple logo in the top left and choosing About This Mac. 
It will clearly show which version of macOS you are running along with the most recent version that your Mac has installed. 
If you are looking for help installing macOS read: How to update macOS and Fixes for Macs that won’t update. We can also help with How to install macOS on an unsupported Mac.





4.
Can I run the macOS beta? 
You can install a beta version of macOS and test new features that haven’t yet launched. If you want to install the latest beta of macOS read about joining Apple’s beta program.





5.
How can I install the latest version of macOS?
Some Macs will be set to update macOS automatically. If you want your Mac to update automatically follow these steps:
Open System Settings.
Click on General. 
Click on Software Update.
Click on the “i” beside Automatic Updates and make sure that Check for updates, Download new updates when available, and Install macOS updates are selected. This way your Mac will automatically update to the latest version. If you would prefer not to have your Mac do this automatically you can deselect these options. 
Read all about how to update your Mac here.





We also have a list of every version of iOS where you can see the latest versions and how long Apple supports iPhones for.

title: Apple HomeView: Everything you need to know about Apple’s smart-home display
content:
Macworld





Apple HomeView is Apple’s first dedicated smart-home display, combining a 7-inch touchscreen, powerful speakers, a camera, and Siri AI in a device designed to sit at the center of the connected home. Announced on October 13, 2026 and on sale from November 13, it brings together smart-home controls, entertainment, video calling, calendars, reminders, and other everyday information.
Powered by Apple’s A18 chip and Apple Intelligence, HomeView offers a much more capable version of Siri that can answer questions conversationally, help with everyday tasks, and access personal information from a compatible iPhone or iPad. It can also recognize up to six members of a household, providing a personalized experience while keeping individual information private.
HomeView is designed to work alongside Apple’s existing HomePod speakers, Apple TV, iPhone, and iPad. It integrates with the Apple Home app, supporting compatible HomeKit and Matter accessories, including lights, locks, thermostats, and security cameras. It can also serve as a central smart-home hub, making it easier to manage devices and automations throughout the house.
Unlike a HomePod with a screen added, HomeView is designed around visual interaction as well as voice control. Its touchscreen, customizable widgets, FaceTime camera, personalized Home Screens, and dedicated smart-home dashboards make it more like a shared household computer than a conventional smart speaker. It comes in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, with prices starting at $299/£299.
What can Apple HomeView do?
HomeView introduces a range of capabilities that aren’t available on Apple’s traditional HomePod speakers. While HomePod focuses primarily on music, Siri, and voice-controlled smart-home functions, HomeView adds a touchscreen, camera, personalized interface, and much deeper integration with Apple apps and services.


FeatureWhat HomeView offers compared to HomePos

Smart-home dashboardTouchscreen controls for lights, locks, heating, scenes, and automations
Siri AIHomeView launches with Siri AI in beta, while HomePod mini 2’s support requires a later update. 
Siri Ai brings: natural conversations, broader knowledge, and personalized assistance with a compatible paired device
Personalized Home ScreenRecognizes up to six users by face and provides individual apps, widgets, and content
FaceTime video callsBuilt-in 12MP Center Stage camera for hands-free video calling
Calendar and remindersView appointments, manage tasks, set timers, and access personal information
Security camerasDisplay up to nine live camera feeds and access intelligent video descriptions
Music and videoView album artwork, lyrics, videos, and supported streaming content on the built-in display
Photos and customizable facesDisplay shared albums, photo collections, clocks, weather, and animated faces
Messages and communicationRead and respond to messages, make calls, and use Intercom
Recipes and household activitiesFollow step-by-step cooking instructions, manage timers, and access helpful information

 



HomeView also supports Handoff from iPhone, Live Activities, Find My, and multiroom audio with compatible AirPlay speakers.
How does HomeView compare with HomePod and iPad?
The biggest difference between HomeView and HomePod is the display. While a HomePod can control smart-home devices and play music using Siri, HomeView provides an interactive dashboard and visual feedback, making it more useful for managing a busy household.
HomeView also offers capabilities that make it a potential alternative to an iPad in certain situations. It can display recipes, calendars, photos, and video calls without needing someone to pick it up or unlock it. Its ability to recognize different household members and switch automatically between personalized experiences is particularly useful in a shared space.
However, HomeView isn’t intended to replace an iPad. The iPad remains the better choice for portable computing, productivity, games, and the broad selection of apps available from the App Store. HomeView is designed to stay in one place and provide convenient access to household information, entertainment, and smart-home controls.


Apple HomeView release date: When will it go on sale?
Announced: October 13, 2026 
Pre-orders: October 13, 2026 
In Store: November 13, 2026
Apple announced HomeView on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, as part of its “Welcome home” launch. Pre-orders opened the same day, with both the tabletop and wall-mounted models scheduled to go on sale on Friday, November 13.
HomeView is initially available in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India, New Zealand, Singapore, and South Africa. Singapore pre-orders open on October 15, while customers in South Africa can order through authorized resellers.
The device won’t initially be sold in the European Union because Siri AI isn’t currently available in iOS in the EU. Apple says it is working toward resolving the situation, but hasn’t announced a European release date.
HomeView can be ordered from the Apple website, Apple Store app, and selected retailers. It will also be displayed in Apple Stores. Apple hasn’t announced any general shipping delays beyond the roughly one-month gap between its announcement and retail availability, although individual delivery estimates may vary.
The November 13 date confirms the mid-November launch timeframe reported before the announcement. Earlier speculation about an October 30 launch is now superseded by Apple’s official schedule.
$299 at  Apple						
					
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.S. 
Pre-order HomeView from Apple U.K. 



Apple HomeView design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			The HomeView from behind

Foundry




HomeView has a compact, square display mounted above a rounded aluminum speaker base, with a design that recalls Apple’s classic iMac G4. A stainless steel hinge allows the screen to tilt, making it easy to adjust the viewing angle when HomeView is positioned on a kitchen counter, desk, or bedside table.
The tabletop model is available in four colors: Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray. The base incorporates the speakers, including a downward-firing woofer, while the display contains two additional full-range drivers. Apple uses 100 percent recycled aluminum in the base and includes a color-matched USB-C power cable.
The wall-mounted HomeView has a different design, with a slim square enclosure that’s just 0.39 inch thick. It is available in Silver and Space Gray and is designed for locations such as hallways and entrances. Unlike the tabletop model, it doesn’t include a separate woofer and requires a compatible wall mount, sold separately.
Both versions feature a touchscreen, built-in camera, four microphones, and USB-C power. Apple hasn’t listed conventional volume or power buttons in the published specifications, with touch and Siri providing the primary controls.





HomeView dimensions and weight


SpecificationTabletop HomeViewHomeView (Wall Mounted)

Width5.73 inches (14.55 cm)5.73 inches (14.55 cm)
Height5.38–6.82 inches (13.67–17.32 cm)5.73 inches (14.55 cm)
Depth3.78–5.13 inches (9.60–13.02 cm)0.39 inch (0.98 cm)
Weight2.1 pounds (952 g)0.63 pound (286 g)
ColorsSilver, Starlight, Rose Pink, Space GraySilver, Space Gray

 The tabletop dimensions vary depending on the display’s tilt angle.






Does Apple HomeView have a camera?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Yes. Both HomeView models feature a built-in 12-megapixel Center Stage camera with an f/2.4 aperture.
The camera supports FaceTime video calling, with Center Stage automatically adjusting the framing to keep people visible as they move around or when additional participants join the conversation. Four beamforming microphones help pick up voices from across the room while reducing background noise.
The built-in camera cannot double as a security camera or provide an Echo Show-style video Drop In feature. HomeView can display feeds from compatible external security cameras, but that is a separate capability.
The camera also plays an important role in HomeView’s personalized features. It can recognize registered household members by face, automatically switching to their individual Home Screen and making their personal information available when the required security conditions are met.
Apple uses a protected processing environment called Secure Exclaves to isolate facial and voice recognition data from the operating system and apps. The system is designed so that the sensitive camera and microphone information used for recognition isn’t exposed to other users or Apple.
Apple hasn’t published more detailed video recording specifications, such as maximum capture resolution or frame rate.






What screen does Apple HomeView have?

				
					

				
			
HomeView

Foundry




HomeView features a 7-inch Liquid Retina touchscreen with a resolution of 1088 by 1088 pixels, giving it a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. It uses an LED-backlit IPS panel with Multi-Touch support, True Tone, and a fingerprint-resistant oleophobic coating.
Maximum brightness reaches 500 nits, while minimum brightness drops to just 0.3 nits, making it suitable for a bedside table without lighting up the room at night.
The interface also adapts to proximity, showing simpler information when viewed from across the room and revealing more detail as someone approaches. Customizable faces include Photos, Calendar, Weather, Flow, and Snoopy.
The display is the same on the tabletop and wall-mounted models. Apple hasn’t specified a refresh rate, and there’s no OLED option.






HomeView audio: Speakers, Dolby Atmos and AirPlay
HomeView combines built-in speakers, Spatial Audio and AirPlay multiroom playback, with additional entertainment and personal features available through a paired iPhone or iPad.
Speakers and sound quality
Both models support Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos for music and video. Each has two full-range drivers in the display, while the tabletop model adds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in its base. The wall-mounted version omits this speaker base, with Apple tuning its computational audio specifically for placement against a wall.
Our initial hands-on impressions placed the tabletop model between the HomePod mini and full-size HomePod for sound: it offered more weight and impact than the mini, while the larger HomePod delivered a bigger sound. These are early impressions; a full review will establish how both HomeView models perform.
Music, apps and multiroom playback
AirPlay lets HomeView join HomePod, HomePod mini and compatible speakers for music playback throughout your home. HomeView also supports FaceTime with Center Stage, Intercom broadcasts, and reading and replying to messages.
Compatible third-party audio and video apps run through your paired device, without requiring installation on HomeView. As our colleague Jason Cross explains, this uses a system based on CarPlay. Support depends on app compatibility, so check your preferred services before buying.
Siri AI and personal features
HomeView’s Siri AI supports conversational questions and music discovery without an Apple Intelligence-capable paired device. Personal-context requests, such as finding information in Messages or Calendar, require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad with Siri AI enabled in a supported language.
To display personal information, HomeView must recognize your face, and your paired device generally needs to be nearby and recently unlocked. This makes your iPhone or iPad an essential part of HomeView’s personalized experience. music throughout your home using HomeView, HomePod, HomePod mini and compatible AirPlay speakers.






What processor does Apple HomeView use?
HomeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, the same generation of processor introduced with the iPhone 16 in 2024. This is considerably more powerful than the Apple Watch-derived processors used in older HomePod models and gives HomeView the processing capabilities needed for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
The A18 is manufactured using a second-generation 3-nanometer process. In its original iPhone implementation, it features a six-core CPU, five-core GPU, and 16-core Neural Engine. Apple hasn’t confirmed whether the HomeView uses exactly the same CPU and GPU configuration, or whether the chip has been adapted for the new device.
The Neural Engine is particularly important because HomeView uses AI to support conversational Siri interactions, recognize household members, process camera and microphone information, and provide personalized responses. Apple’s Secure Exclaves also isolate sensitive recognition data from the operating system and applications.
Apple hasn’t revealed any performance comparisons between HomeView and previous HomePod processors, or disclosed any HomeView-specific improvements to chip packaging or manufacturing. However, the A18’s efficient 3nm architecture should help Apple deliver substantial processing power in a compact device that’s designed to operate continuously.
The A18 was one of the key specifications correctly predicted in our earlier HomeView rumors.





Apple HomeView connectivity and compatibility
HomeView supports Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread networking, giving it the wireless connectivity needed to communicate with Apple devices and compatible smart-home accessories.

HomeView integrates directly with Apple’s Home app and can control compatible smart lights, door locks, thermostats, blinds, and security cameras. It also supports Matter accessories, expanding compatibility beyond devices specifically designed for HomeKit.
Importantly, HomeView can act as a home hub itself. You don’t need to buy a separate HomePod or Apple TV simply to use HomeView as your smart-home hub. However, some advanced features depend on compatible accessories, an iCloud+ subscription, or an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. 
Apple has also announced the Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of cameras, thermostats, and a smart lock developed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The first accessories will arrive in December 2026, with additional products following in early 2027.


Which iPhones and iPads work with HomeView?
Apple lists an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later or an iPad running iPadOS 27.2 or later as a system requirement, alongside Wi-Fi internet access.
To use HomeView’s more personalized Siri AI features, you’ll need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Basic Siri AI functions, including general questions and conversational interactions, remain available without an Apple Intelligence-enabled companion device. Siri AI must be enabled on the paired device and set to a supported language, though.
HomeView also requires an Apple Account and compatible paired device for each household member who wants access to their personal information.






Does Apple HomeView have a battery or MagSafe charging?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Neither HomeView model has a built-in battery. Both are designed to remain connected to a power supply, so you can’t pick one up and use it around the house like an iPad.
The standard tabletop model includes a 1.5-meter USB-C cable and a 30W power adapter. Its USB-C connection supplies power rather than functioning as a conventional charging port.
The wall-mounted HomeView also requires continuous power, but Apple doesn’t include the wall mount, USB-C cable, or power adapter. These must be purchased separately, with a minimum 20W power adapter required when using a compatible USB-C power arrangement.
Apple offers three mounting solutions through Schneider Home, including a plug-in USB-C option, an AC-wired installation, and a Power over Ethernet (PoE) version coming in early 2027.






What software does Apple HomeView use?

				
					

				
			
Like a big Apple Watch

Apple




HomeView runs dedicated home-focused software built around Siri AI, Apple’s Home app, widgets, and a selection of familiar Apple applications. Apple identifies the initial Siri AI software as HomeView software version 27.2.
Rather than providing a conventional iPad interface, HomeView is designed to show useful information at a glance and respond to touch, voice, and proximity. Users can customize their Home Screen with apps and widgets, while special faces display photos, clocks, weather, calendar information, and animated artwork.
What can Siri AI do on HomeView?
Siri AI is one of HomeView’s biggest selling points. Powered by Apple Intelligence, it can answer open-ended questions, understand follow-up requests, draw on broad world knowledge, and support natural conversations.
For example, users can ask Siri to find a recipe, explain something they’re interested in, recommend music, control their smart-home accessories, or help organize everyday tasks.
When HomeView is paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, Siri becomes more personal. It can draw on information from Calendar, Messages, and other apps, helping users locate an invitation, check an appointment, or find relevant information without manually searching their devices.
Siri conversations can also continue across Apple devices using the Siri app, with conversation history privately synced through iCloud.
There are some limitations. Siri AI initially supports English, with Canadian French coming later. Certain AI features that use server-side models have daily usage limits, and Apple says expanded access will eventually be available for a fee. Siri AI launches in beta on HomeView software 27.2.





Which apps are available on HomeView?
Apple includes a selection of built-in apps and provides access to additional entertainment services through compatible iPhones.

HomeView supports third-party audio and video apps from compatible iPhones, but Apple hasn’t announced a dedicated HomeView App Store or general installation of iPad apps. That means it shouldn’t be regarded as a replacement for an iPad’s broader software capabilities.


How does HomeView work for different family members?
HomeView can recognize up to six users by their faces, automatically switching between personalized Home Screens and keeping each person’s content separate.
For example, one family member could approach HomeView and see their own calendar and reminders, while another would be shown different information. Shared photo albums, music, and general smart-home controls can still be enjoyed by everyone.
Access to personal information is more tightly controlled. The user’s paired iPhone or iPad must be on the same Wi-Fi network, must have been recently unlocked, and HomeView must recognize the person’s face.
Guests and unrecognized users can still ask Siri questions, play music, check the weather, set timers, and control eligible smart-home accessories, without gaining access to anyone’s private messages or calendars.






Is Apple HomeView secure?
Apple has designed HomeView with a particular emphasis on privacy, given that it includes an always-available camera and microphones in a shared household space. There is no physical camera/microphone privacy switch, but you can disable them via software controls.
The A18 chip uses Secure Exclaves to process camera and microphone data used for recognizing faces and voices. This information is isolated from the operating system and apps, so sensitive recognition data isn’t exposed to other software or Apple.
For Siri requests, HomeView can process information locally or use Private Cloud Compute, which Apple says handles cloud requests without storing the data or making it accessible to Apple.
HomeView also supports HomeKit Secure Video, including intelligent recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles with a compatible iCloud+ subscription. It can provide AI-generated descriptions of recorded activity, although these advanced features require setup with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.






How much does Apple HomeView cost?
Apple HomeView $299/£299
Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) $299/£299
Apple HomeView starts at $299 in the U.S. and £299 in the U.K., with the tabletop and wall-mounted models carrying the same base price.
This positions HomeView below the $349 full-size HomePod price, although HomeView isn’t necessarily a direct replacement for that audio-focused speaker. 





Do HomeView wall mounts cost extra?
Yes. While the tabletop HomeView includes the accessories needed for power, the wall-mounted version requires additional purchases.

For U.S. customers, this brings the minimum hardware cost of the wall-mounted HomeView and listed USB-C mount to $358.95/£353.95, before any additional installation or power accessories.


Is a larger HomeView coming?
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple is developing a higher-end HomeView, codenamed J595, for a possible 2027 or 2028 release. It could feature a 9-inch display and a motorized arm offering 360-degree movement, allowing the screen to turn toward the speaker. Apple has not confirmed the product or its name; “Max” and “Ultra” are speculative. These rumored features are not part of the 7-inch HomeView scheduled to go on sale on November 13, 2026.






Should you buy Apple HomeView?
Apple HomeView looks particularly appealing for households already invested in Apple’s ecosystem. It brings together smart-home controls, a capable Siri assistant, video calling, entertainment, and personalized information in a single device that can be shared by everyone at home.
For families, its biggest advantage could be convenience. Being able to see calendars, reminders, weather, timers, and security cameras in a central location, while automatically switching between household members, makes HomeView more useful than a conventional smart speaker.
It’s also attractive for people with extensive HomeKit or Matter smart-home setups. Rather than relying on an iPhone whenever they want to adjust the heating, check a security camera, or activate a scene, users get a dedicated interface that’s always available.
However, HomeView won’t be essential for everyone. If you mainly use Siri to play music, set timers, and control a handful of smart lights, a HomePod mini is a considerably cheaper option. And if you already use an iPad on a stand in the kitchen, you may find that it handles many of the same tasks while offering much greater flexibility.
At $299/£299, HomeView is a premium alternative to smart displays from Amazon and Google. Its strongest selling points are its integration with Apple products, privacy-focused recognition of individual users, and the more powerful Siri AI experience. However, it’s worth remembering that some of those personalized AI features require a recent Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.






Which HomeView model should you buy?
For most people, the standard tabletop HomeView is the more sensible choice. It costs the same as the wallmounted version but includes a more substantial speaker system, an adjustable display, and the power accessories needed to get started.
The wallmounted version makes more sense if you want a permanent smarthome control panel in a hallway, entrance, or other shared area. Its slim design is more discreet, although the additional cost of mounting accessories and potentially professional installation makes it less affordable.
We’d recommend waiting for independent reviews before deciding whether HomeView’s sound quality, Siri performance, and personalized features justify its price. But for Apple households looking for a central smart-home display, HomeView already offers a combination of features that no existing HomePod can match.

title: Apple Store Subscription Sign-Up Controversy Exposed
content:
In a series of YouTube videos shared over the past two weeks, electronics technician and consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann has exposed a controversy in which some Apple Store employees have allegedly signed up customers for auto-renewing subscription trials for Apple One and other services without their informed consent.


Here is how the process works at Apple Stores in the United States:
A customer visits an Apple Store.

An employee at the store asks if the customer would like to scan a QR code for a personalized shopping experience ("Connect and Personalize").

If the customer agrees, the employee can view some of the customer's information on their company-issued device, including which Apple devices they own, which Apple services they are subscribed to, and which Apple subscription offers are available to them based on their recent purchases.

The employee can proceed to show the customer their available subscription offers, presented with "Agree" and "Decline" buttons on the employee's device. The default payment method associated with the customer's Apple Account is automatically available for subscription sign-ups, so long as it has not expired.
The problem is that some employees allegedly activated these trials without adequately explaining to the customers that they would be automatically charged at a later date, according to tipsters who contacted Rossmann. For example, some employees would allegedly rush through the process or were even told to position the trials as "gifts."

Until early last week, Apple was tracking a metric known as the "services attach rate," with a target of 40% for each retail employee at at least some U.S. stores. In other words, employees were encouraged to get at least four out of every 10 customers they assisted with a device purchase to also sign up for at least one subscription.

In some cases, employees allegedly even tapped the "Agree" button themselves without receiving the customer's informed consent, seemingly in an attempt to ensure that their "services attach rate" was as high as possible.

"Top performers in my store and market just include them and don't show the customer the accept/decline screen during checkout," one anonymous person alleged. "I've confirmed with others that this happens at other stores, and I've had many employees admit to me that they do this. It is unfortunate that this is our culture now."

Apple does email customers when a new trial has been activated on their accounts, but unsuspecting customers might not pay attention or realize that the email pertains to a subscription that will automatically renew later.

Metric Removed, Reminder Issued

MacRumors has confirmed that Apple removed the services metric for employees early last week, just days after Rossmann's videos were published. However, the official explanation we were given for the metric's removal is that it is less relevant during the holiday season, when customers are often purchasing Apple products as gifts for others.

Later in the week, Apple issued an internal memo to retail employees reminding them of the importance of respecting customer privacy and obtaining consent, including when offering subscription trials and using the "Connect and Personalize" system, but also for things such as Apple Upgrade sign-ups and Genius Bar work authorizations.

kicked off on Friday. During the holidays, Apple hires additional employees to help assist with an influx of customers, so the reminder was timely for new staff.

Whether these actions were timed solely around the holiday shopping season or were also influenced by Rossmann's videos, we cannot say for sure. In any case, the actions conveniently address some of the concerns highlighted by Rossmann.

How to Check Your Subscriptions

On an iPhone, open the Settings app and tap on your name at the top of the screen. Next, tap on "Subscriptions" and you will see a list of any subscriptions that are active on your Apple Account, including trials. You can tap on any individual subscription and tap on the "Cancel Subscription" or "Cancel All Services" button to cancel.

reportaproblem.apple.com, select the "Request a refund" option, and follow the steps.

title: Apple Taking New Approach to Developing iOS 28 and macOS 28
content:
Apple has made a change to its development process for iOS 28, macOS 28, and corresponding software updates, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.


In his Power On newsletter today, he said Apple separates development of each year's new operating systems into three major stages. Typically, he said each stage consists of four weeks of coding followed by a four-week "convergence" period where new features are integrated into the operating systems. This time around, Apple has made a change.

The first stage of development for iOS 28 and the other updates apparently consisted of six weeks of coding and two weeks of feature convergence. This change gives Apple's software engineers more time to come up with new features.

"Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence," he said. "Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in."

title: I’m a believer in Touch after using Apple’s new PROLED MacBook Pro
content:
Macworld





Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display isn’t just the best display ever put in a laptop. It’s also Apple’s first-ever touchscreen in a Mac and the first time macOS has supported Touch as an input option. It’s a feature we longtime Mac users thought we’d never see, mostly because Apple has a history of saying it won’t happen.
But it has happened—and on the most expensive laptop Apple sells, no less. It’s $400 more than the non-Touch MacBook Pro, and the model I tested has customized specs that bring the price to $7,399. While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has plenty of other features to attract customers, the touchscreen is one of the most interesting features to come to the Mac in years and is sure to be a major consideration for buyers when choosing which laptop to get.
However, macOS with Touch isn’t the same interface that you can just reach out to control with your fingers. Apple has enhanced and optimized macOS to accommodate Touch, making the overall experience satisfying. This article details the macOS Touch experience; you can read my full review of the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED Display here.
No lag or delay
Apple did not simply take a Touch input sensor, slap it on top of the OLED, pack it all up, and ship it. For the optimal experience, the Touch sensor is incorporated into the OLED panel, just as it is with the iPad Pro. That makes it perform more like a tablet than a usual touchscreen laptop.

				
					

				
			
Touch is very responsive, with no noticeable delay between a gesture and response.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




It also means there’s no lag when touching the screen. Tap the screen, and you’ll get an instant reaction from macOS: buttons, menus, sliders, icons, the Dock, you name it. Everything reacts the instant you touch it.
UI clarity
My major concern about the touchscreen MacBook Pro was whether Apple would do enough (or anything) to adjust macOS’s longstanding UI elements for Touch input. Some elements in macOS need to be larger to make them easier to touch; others need to be shifted to create more space; and still others need a complete rethink. A touch UI that demands cursor-style precision means you have to concentrate to do the most mundane of tasks. That’s tiring.

				
					

				
			Left: Contextual menu when using the trackpad. Right: Contextual menu when using Touch.
Foundry




In macOS 27.2 on the new MacBook Pro, Apple has enhanced macOS to accommodate Touch. Throughout the OS, elements appear when using Touch and return to the normal view when using a mouse or trackpad. The first thing you’ll notice is the set of traffic lights that appear in the upper right corner of windows to close, minimize, or expand windows full-screen, respectively. When tapped, the red, yellow, and green buttons magnify to make the target easier to hit.
Even menu items adjust by expanding a bit to add space between the items so they’re easier to tap with your finger. Another example is checkboxes, which let you tap on the accompanying text to select as well as the box itself.

				
					

				
			
Traffic lights are enlarged to make them easier to touch.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




UI confusion
Almost all of the time, I can navigate through macOS just by using Touch. Apple thoughtfully considered the elements that I encountered to make them easy to touch, with one exception: video files. The ability to watch a tiny version of the video by clicking on the “Play” icon in the center of the video’s icon gets in the way of opening the file. Double-tapping to open the video file often resulted in the video playing in the icon, not actually opening the file. It’s one of the things that hasn’t been adjusted to accommodate Touch, and it needs a retool.
I also found that the mindset for Touch on macOS is separate from iOS. My experience with Apple’s touch-based UI is mostly with iOS, so I thought that macOS Touch would work similarly. But Apple decided to stick to macOS conventions, as illustrated by opening an app. In iOS, opening an app is a single tap. In macOS, a single tap selects the app, just as a single click does with a mouse or trackpad. You need to double-tap to launch the app.

				
					

				
			
Even enlarging the icons to 128-by-128 pixels didn’t make opening video files any easier.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Gesture support
Multi-Touch gestures on the Mac support the same gestures that are on the trackpad and, for the most part, your iPhone and iPad. It’s all smart and effortless, especially if you already use these gestures on a trackpad: Swipe with two fingers to scroll up, down, left, or right.  Use three fingers and swipe left or right to switch desktops. A four-finger swipe up opens Mission Control. A four-finger swipe down opens App Exposé, etc.
Pinch-to-zoom even works. Rotate, where you use two fingers in a rotating motion, also works, but this gesture was awkward for me to do on a standing screen. I think it’s easier to do on a trackpad or, say, an iPad that’s lying flat.

				
					

				
			
Rotate gestures are supported, but not always comfortable to do.

Roman Loyola/Foundry




Screen wobble
Apple re-engineered the MacBook Pro’s hinge to make the screen more stable while touching it. The hinge provides enough resistance when you’re pressing relatively softly against the screen. Push hard enough, and the screen falls back, but most of the time, you’re not going to need to push that hard. In the animation above, you can see the screen wobble as I do the rotation gesture, but it’s exaggerated since I repeated the gesture several times and inadvertently pressed harder than usual.
If you tap lightly, you won’t see the display move, but most people will tap hard enough to see a wobble. However, my regular taps caused the display to shake slightly, which was noticeable but bearable. The wobble is significantly less than a regular MacBook Pro, however, and after the first few taps, I barely noticed it.
Fingerprints
It’s a consequence of using any touchscreen: the display will end up with fingerprints smeared all over it. Like an iPad, they’re not noticeable when the display is on, but when the display goes dark or turns off, ugh. It’s gross.

				
					

				
			Fingerprints are unavoidable.
Roman Loyola/Foundry




This is just a fact about touchscreens we have to live with. Even with Apple’s oleophobic coating, there just isn’t a practical way to prevent fingerprints from appearing at all. There are personal habits that can be practiced to minimize the mess: clean your hands before using the touchscreen, wipe your hands frequently, don’t eat while using a touchscreen, etc. Or you could use touch-friendly gloves, or even wear latex gloves (I tried it and it works), but that’s not practical (and it’s ridiculous). Have a microfiber cloth handy to clean the display; Apple unfortunately doesn’t include one unless you spring for the nano-texture coating, but they sell one for $9. Amazon sells a six-pack of Koala Lens Cleaning Cloths for $10.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display’s Touch works only with fingers, not with an Apple Pencil or any third-party stylus. Other than fingerprints, using your fingers doesn’t offer nearly the same precision as using a stylus, so it’s closer to using an iPhone rather than an iPad or a graphics tablet.
A very good start
Apple isn’t marketing the MacBook Pro as a Touch-first device. Rather, Touch is something users can turn to when the situation calls for it. But it’s promising nonetheless. This first version of the Mac’s Touch UI is smooth, reliable, usable, and even fun. It’s a good start, and I hope Apple invents ways to take advantage of Touch, evolving it beyond being a touch interface on top of macOS.

title: 'Backglow' Lets You Customize New MacBook Pro's Glowing Apple Logo
content:
A new "Backglow" app created by designer Juan Buis lets you customize the illuminated Apple logo on the lid of the new MacBook Pro models.


The free version of the app allows you to manually adjust the brightness level of the Apple logo, independent of the MacBook Pro's display brightness level. You can also turn it off entirely with a single click, rather than having to use Terminal.

Another free option is a "Breathe" mode that makes the logo's light gently pulse similarly to the sleep indicator light on older MacBooks.

A one-time payment unlocks the Pro version of the app: $9 for a limited time or $15 later. This gives you two additional modes: "Music" mode makes the logo's light move to the beat of the music you play on your Mac, while "Agents" mode makes the light pulse while Claude Code is working and blinks when your attention is needed.


here's what it can do:

- manually set logo brightness (apple doesn't let you)
- breathe slowly, like the old mac sleep light
- pulse to your music
- blink when claude needs you
- turn the logo light off with one click

— juan (@juanbuis) November 6, 2026



Apple began phasing out the glowing logo on MacBooks in 2015, but it brought back the feature with the new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with PROLED XDR displays released on Friday. On older MacBooks, the logo was illuminated by the display's backlight, but OLED displays do not have a backlight, so a new method was required.

Daring Fireball's John Gruber was told that Apple engineered a "custom light source just to enable the logo to glow once again, without adding any additional thickness to the lid." Why? "Because it's awesome," he heard an Apple representative say.

says the logo is illuminated whenever the Mac is awake. It automatically brightens or dims based on the screen's brightness level and your environment's lighting conditions detected by the computer's ambient light sensor.

Our Verdict 
The Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless combines excellent sound, firm bass, and improved noise cancellation with outstanding battery life. Its lightweight, padded design stays comfortable during long listening sessions, while USB-C and analog connections add flexibility. The AirPods Max still has an edge when blocking higher-frequency noise, but the Momentum 5 costs considerably less and lasts far longer between charges.

What are they? Comfortable wireless over-ear headphones with excellent sound, improved noise cancellation, and long battery life.
Who are they best for? Travelers and frequent listeners seeking great sound and longer battery life for less than AirPods Max.
Who should skip them? Bargain hunters who can save with the Momentum 4, or buyers prioritizing the strongest noise cancellation.
The Momentum 4 was already one of our favourite over-ear headphones, and the new Momentum 5 provides a number of improvements that help to improve both sound quality and noise-cancellation. This update is a little more expensive though, now costing $399.95/£329.99, although the Momentum 4 is still widely available online with a reduced price of around $299.00/£199.00 so that’s still a good option if you’re looking for a bargain.
Available in a variety of colours, the Momentum 5 looks very similar to its predecessor, with large earpieces that house 42mm drivers and are thickly padded for comfort. Despite the large earpieces, the headphone only weighs 290g – compared to 386g for Apple’s AirPods Max – so they’re light and comfortable enough to wear for long periods of time, and Sennheiser also includes a sturdy travelling case to protect the headphones when you’re out and about. Battery life is impressive too, lasting for around 57 hours even when using noise-cancellation – compared to just 20 hours for the AirPods Max – which makes the Momentum 5 a great option for long journeys. And, if the battery does run down then you can switch to wired mode, with both USB-C and 3.5mm cables included (although the 3.5mm cable has a 2.5mm jack for connecting to the headphones, which could cause problems if you lose the cable and need to buy a replacement).
Bluetooth support has been updated for this model, stepping up to Bluetooth 5.4 and aptX Lossless/Adaptive, along with AAC for Apple devices, and support for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. The Momentum 5 is also certified for hi-res audio, and provides an impressive frequency response of 6Hz – 40KHz when using Bluetooth or a USB-C connection, which results in excellent sound quality.
It digs really deep for the rumbling electronic bass effects on Max Richter’s Shadow Journal, while the spatial audio creates an atmospheric soundstage for the track’s hazy, ambient sounds. There’s clarity on the higher frequencies too, with the violins cutting through haze to add a sense of urgency to the piece. Switching to something heavier and harder, the Momentum 5 does a great job of balancing the sonic mash-up of Sing Along by Sturgill Simpson. The fuzzy guitar riffs have a head-banging power that drives the track forward, while the precise, ticking percussion is irresistibly catchy. The synths wail with dance-floor energy, and the bass drop toward the end has a real kick to it.
The noise-cancellation has been improved as well. The Momentum 5 can now match the AirPods Max when it comes to blocking out low-frequency sounds such as the rumble of an aircraft engine. It does a good job with higher frequency sounds too, although the AirPods Max still has an edge in that area. Mind you, the AirPods Max are around $200/£200 more expensive so the Momentum 5 is really good value for money, especially with that outstanding battery life for long journeys.
Should you buy the Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless? 
The Momentum 5 Wireless is a strong choice if you want excellent sound, effective noise cancellation, and enough battery life for long journeys. Its deep, firm bass brings energy to electronic music and rock, while clear higher frequencies keep instruments distinct. The lightweight design and generous padding also make it comfortable for extended listening.
For Apple users, AAC support, Dolby Atmos spatial audio, and USB-C audio provide useful flexibility. Noise cancellation matches the AirPods Max for low-frequency rumble, although Apple’s headphones retain an advantage with higher-frequency sounds. The Momentum 5 counters with a considerably lower price and around 57 hours of battery life with noise cancellation enabled.
At $399.95/£329.99, it offers a compelling balance of sound, comfort, and endurance. However, bargain hunters should consider the Momentum 4, available for around $299/£199. The improved sound and noise cancellation make the newer model appealing, but the older headphones remain a good budget option.

Buying advice: What to look for when buying headphones
Below, we run through what to look for when choosing over-ear headphones for your iPhone or Mac, from sound quality and comfort to Apple features, lossless audio, noise cancellation and battery life.






Which headphone features matter for iPhone and Mac users?
Sound quality, comfort and reliable connectivity should come first. AAC support is useful for Bluetooth listening on Apple devices, but it isn’t required for basic compatibility. Check which additional features work with your iPhone, iPad and Mac, including easy pairing, automatic switching, hands-free Siri and Find My. These vary between models – even within Apple’s AirPods and Beats ranges.
Bluetooth multipoint lets compatible headphones maintain connections to two devices, making it useful for moving between an iPhone and Mac. Check how switching works in practice, rather than assuming it behaves like Apple’s automatic switching. Also check whether the manufacturer’s iPhone app offers equalizer controls and firmware updates.
Prioritize listening assessments over driver size or frequency-response claims. Look for clear vocals, audible detail and bass that suits your taste without overwhelming the music.






Can I listen to Apple Music lossless through headphones?
Yes, but the connection matters. Standard Bluetooth playback from an iPhone or Mac uses compression, even when you select a lossless track in Apple Music. A compatible wired connection is the straightforward way to hear lossless audio.
AirPods Max 2 and the first-generation USB-C AirPods Max support lossless playback over USB-C with current software and firmware. Some competing wireless headphones, including Beats Studio Pro, also offer USB audio. However, a USB-C charging port doesn’t necessarily support audio, so check before buying.
Traditional headphones with a 3.5mm plug are another option. Depending on your device, you may need an adapter or an external digital-to-analog converter (DAC). The supported resolution depends on the entire connection; wired listening doesn’t automatically guarantee support for Apple Music’s highest-resolution recordings. See our guide to DACs and lossless audio on iPhone and Mac.
Some headphones include a wireless transmitter. Check its compatibility and supported formats: adding a transmitter doesn’t automatically make playback lossless.






How much noise cancellation do I need?
For frequent flights, train journeys or noisy workplaces, prioritize effective active noise cancellation (ANC). It is particularly useful against steady sounds such as engine drone. Performance against conversations and sudden noises varies, so look for listening-test results rather than relying on manufacturers’ claims.
Passive isolation comes from the earcups sealing around your ears. A good fit helps both isolation and sound quality. Transparency or ambient modes use microphones to let you hear your surroundings without removing the headphones – useful when listening for announcements or maintaining awareness while walking.
If you make frequent calls, assess microphone performance separately: effective listening ANC doesn’t guarantee clear speech for the person you’re calling.






What makes over-ear headphones comfortable?
Comfort depends on weight, clamping pressure, headband design and earcup cushioning. Lighter headphones aren’t automatically more comfortable: how the headband distributes weight matters, too.
Look for enough adjustment to position the earcups comfortably around your ears, with a secure fit that doesn’t squeeze. Glasses can affect both comfort and the seal. Cushion materials also matter, particularly if heat and sweating become uncomfortable during longer sessions.
Try headphones for an extended session if possible, checking for pressure around your ears and across your head. For travel, consider whether they fold and whether the supplied case provides adequate protection.






How much battery life do I need?
Choose enough battery life for your longest listening sessions, with some allowance for missed charges. Around 30 hours with ANC enabled is a useful target for commuting and occasional travel, while frequent travelers may prefer longer endurance. A shorter runtime can still be sufficient if you recharge regularly.
Compare figures under the same conditions: turning off ANC can substantially increase battery life. Our reviews distinguish manufacturers’ estimates from measured results where available.
Quick charging can be as useful as total endurance, providing enough playback for a journey after a short charge. For longer trips, check whether headphones work while charging or through a cable with an empty battery. Wired listening doesn’t necessarily mean battery-free listening.






What is Auracast?
Auracast lets a compatible source broadcast audio to multiple headphones or hearing devices. It can be useful for shared listening or receiving audio in equipped public venues. Check explicitly for Auracast reception support; a recent Bluetooth version alone doesn’t guarantee it.





How Macworld reviews headphones
When our audio experts review headphones our comprehensive evaluation covers sound quality, design and comfort, key features like noise cancellation, and overall value for money. We undertake subjective listening tests and an objective analysis of features and build quality. 
The most critical aspect of our headphone reviews is an assessment of audio performance including Tonal Balance, Clarity and Detail, Audio Defects and Spatial Audio. 
Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency Modes are also assessed, both being primary features users look for. We test how effectively the headphones block out different types of ambient sound, such as the low-frequency drone of an airplane engine versus higher-frequency chatter. We also assess how well transparency mode amplify outside sounds when you need to be aware of your surroundings.
Design, comfort and build quality are also important factors, as is the ease of use when it comes to the controls and functionality. Battery life is another important consideration, and the time it takes to charge the headphones. 
Finally, we review the available connection options and the codecs supported since AAC support is required for Apple devices.

title: Revealed: Apple’s secret list of slurs, insults, and political phrases that can’t be swiped
content:
Macworld





According to a research project by Derik Kauffman, Apple has a built-in list of words and phrases that the keyboard suggested words will never complete, and the swiping keyboard will not produce. This isn’t a censorship list—typing individual characters always works—but it can slow you down if you’re looking to use swiping or suggested words to speed up your iPhone typing.
The project is detailed at Swipeblocked.com, with additional code and data hosted on GitHub. There, Kauffman details his forensics to discover this feature and the blocked phrases.
Here’s how it works: Apple has built into iOS a hash table of “blocked” phrases. It’s not storing plain text of words, but rather matching hashes of word IDs to a set of banned hashes. If there’s a match, the iOS keyboard will not suggest the word. And if you are swiping, it will either input some other word for your swiped word or replace an earlier word in your phrase with a different word that has a similar swipe pattern.
The list of phrases has not been made public by Apple, and the company does not disclose how it chooses what goes on it. Kauffman reverse-engineered it from the hash table within iOS.
The phrases are mostly what you would expect. They include vulgarities, politically and socially charged phrases, rascist terms, various forms of bigotry, and so on. You can literally type out the phrase, “smoking weed,” but if you type “smoking wee…” then the keyboard suggestions to finish off that second word will never include the obvious “weed.” Instead, you’ll get “weekend” or “weekly.” And if you’re using Apple’s QuickPath (Slide to Type), you’ll get “smoking Wed” or some other word, no matter how precise you are about swiping the word “weed” correctly.
The Swipeblocked site has a list of all the English-language banned phrases in iOS 27. Warning: Many of them are not safe for work and highly offensive. But some are things that you may very well wish to type or swipe, especially in a particular context (illegal immigrant, NBA surveillance, etc.), and the refusal of the iOS keyboard to complete swiping entry or suggest the natural next word is one reason users are frustrated with it.
In addition to the phrases that are blocked from the suggested word area or swiping, there is a mechanism to prevent the autocomplete and suggested word list from suggesting individual words. The iOS dictionary labels words as either vulgar, offensive, or sensitive. Vulgar words are not suggested until the user manually types them three times. Offensive words are never suggested or completed by swiping (though you can always type them out yourself). Sensitive words are similarly never offered as a prediction or completion, and some of them can’t be swiped.
Why does Apple do all this? It’s likely less about policing your speech than it is about avoiding lawsuits and bad PR. All it takes is one person posting a screenshot of the iOS keyboard suggesting the word “good” after they type “The Nazis were” or “real” after Santa isn’t” (both included in the list) to cause a bad viral moment criticizing Apple’s intentions, even if the keyboard suggestions would only suggest things that the user had typed several times before.
However, it’s still overreaching. A good solution would be to give users a choice. Allow a keyboard setting, enabled by default, to moderate the suggested word list and swipe keyboard to avoid offensive content, but also give users the ability to turn it off. But until then, you’ll need to type a little more slowly if you want to write certain phrases.

title: Top Stories: Apple Product Launches, iOS 27.3 Beta, and More
content:
Apple is still rocking and rolling a week into November, with five new products having launched this week and two more still on tap for next week.


Things are also moving forward on the software side with Apple releasing the first betas of iOS 27.3 and related updates, bringing a number of tweaks and new features. We're also looking ahead to new products coming in the first half of 2027, so read on below for all of the details on these stories and more!

Top Stories

Apple Launched Five New Products This Week

Apple released five new products on Friday, November 6, following pre-orders that opened last week, including its first touchscreen MacBook Pro models.


The following new products are now available:

iPad mini with OLED display and A20 Pro chip

iMac with M6 chip

14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 chip

14-inch MacBook Pro with OLED touchscreen

16-inch MacBook Pro with OLED touchscreen


will follow next week on Friday, November 13.

Everything New in the iOS 27.3 Beta

Apple this week started testing iOS 27.3, the biggest update to iOS 27 since it launched in September. iOS 27.3 includes some features Apple showed off earlier this year, and it adds all-new capabilities.


Among the changes in the update are Safari tweaks with a new Vertical Tabs layout option plus an Adaptive Dark Mode feature for websites that don't offer their own dark mode option, Siri AI improvements, an expansion of new iPhone Duo StandBy features to other iPhone models, and more.

revamped Health app that was in the 27.2 beta for testing but removed prior to the public release has returned in 27.3 and will be seeing a public launch before the end of the year.

Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue

In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers last week, and later obtained by MacRumors, Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue.


If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance.

not able to predict when it will be able to meet demand for the foldable iPhone, with Bloomberg's Mark Gurman saying that Apple's change from its original plan to launch the device in November in just two countries has contributed to the difficulties in meeting demand.

Three New iPads Rumored to Launch in First Half of 2027

The revamped iPad mini launching this week is one piece of Apple's tablet lineup, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman says the rest of the lineup should be receiving updates in the first half of next year. The iPad Air will reportedly be getting an upgrade to OLED displays, while iPad Pro and base iPad updates should be more modest.


Before those 2027 updates, there's still some time left in 2026, and while we're not expecting any more major product announcements before the end of the year, plenty of previously announced hardware and software updates are still on their way.

Here's a New Tour of Apple's HomeView Software

App developer Steve Troughton-Smith over the weekend shared a tour of the software on Apple's upcoming HomeView smart home hub. Apple has already demoed the HomeView to selected tech reporters and content creators, but Troughton-Smith offered a closer look at several features, interfaces, and apps.


CarPlay-enabled audio and video apps from third-party developers will also be supported on HomeView, and Troughton-Smith shared a look at what Spotify will look like on the HomeView as well.

initially ship with six-month-old software version 26.5 and will have to be updated to HomeView software version 27.2 during setup.

Apple's Flash Storage Suppliers Are Finally 'Getting Their Revenge'

The Wall Street Journal's Rolfe Winkler last week reported that flash storage suppliers once "bullied" by Apple have been "getting their revenge" on the company over the past year due to a severe memory chip shortage, which stems from AI companies building out massive data centers that utilize significant amounts of flash storage and RAM.


As the iPhone took off, Apple became the world's largest buyer of flash storage, and naturally that gave the company a lot of leverage in negotiations. The report goes into detail about some of the hardball tactics that were employed by Apple and its former head of procurement, Tony Blevins.

Flash suppliers now have the upper hand, however, and high demand for their chips has resulted in shortages that are expected to persist through 2030 with high prices continuing as a result.

title: JBL Cove M1 review: Compact AirPlay 2 speaker, big sound
content:
Macworld





At a glance
Expert's Rating



Pros
Lively, detailed sound with impressive volume
Compact design fits desks and shelves
AirPlay 2, Bluetooth, and stereo pairing
Cons
Deep bass lacks weight and precision

Our Verdict 
The JBL Cove M1 combines lively, detailed sound and impressive volume with a compact design. AirPlay 2, Bluetooth, stereo pairing, and multiroom support make it a versatile choice for Apple users. Deep bass lacks weight and there are no wired audio inputs, but at $229.95/£199.99, it offers good value for everyday listening on a desk or shelf in smaller rooms.
