Its main appeal in the current lineup, however, is price: it only makes sense when discounted significantly below the newer models.
Buy iPhone 16 if
Buy the iPhone 16 if you find it heavily discounted and want Apple Intelligence, a capable dual-camera system and features such as Camera Control and the Action button without paying for the latest generation.
Don’t buy iPhone 16 if
Don’t buy it at full price. The iPhone 17e offers newer hardware, twice the base storage and longer battery life for less, while the iPhone 17 is considerably more advanced for only a little more money.
What do you get that you don’t get with the iPhone 17e?
The iPhone 16 has a second 12MP Ultra Wide camera, giving it greater photographic versatility, as well as Camera Control and the Action button. Those features may make it preferable to the 17e for photography-minded buyers, but only if the price is right.
What do you miss compared with the iPhone 17?
The iPhone 17 gives you a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion Always-On display, newer A19 processor, upgraded 48MP Ultra Wide camera, improved 18MP Centre Stage selfie camera, longer battery life and 256GB of storage as standard. Unless the iPhone 16 is heavily discounted, the 17 is easily worth the difference.
Key specs
The iPhone 16 combines the A18 chip with a 48MP Fusion Main camera, 12MP Ultra Wide camera, Camera Control, the Action button and Apple Intelligence support. It remains a capable smartphone, but its 128GB starting storage and older display make it less compelling than the newer iPhone 17e and iPhone 17.
Starts at: $799 / £799 (was $699 / £699) for 128GB
Display: 6.1-inch Super Retina XDR OLED
Chip: A18
Storage: 128GB–512GB
Cameras: 48MP Main + 12MP Ultra Wide
Battery: Up to 22 hours of video playback
Should you buy or wait?
Don’t buy at full price. Only consider the iPhone 16 if it’s heavily discounted below the iPhone 17e; otherwise, Apple’s newer models offer substantially better value.

							
		


Which iPhone has the best camera? iPhone 18 Pro

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both models use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.
The headline upgrade is the 48MP Main camera with variable aperture, which gives photographers more control over depth of field and should improve low-light performance. The Pro models also include a 48MP Ultra Wide camera and a 48MP Telephoto camera with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom, giving them far more flexibility than Apple’s cheaper iPhones.
The standard iPhone 17 is still an excellent camera phone, with 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras, plus an improved 18MP Centre Stage front camera. For everyday photography it will be more than enough for most people, but it lacks the dedicated telephoto lens, longer zoom and advanced video features of the Pro models.
The iPhone Duo is more compromised. Despite its premium price, it has only two 48MP rear cameras and lacks a dedicated telephoto camera, variable aperture, ProRes and Apple Log. Its strengths are instead its fold-specific shooting features and dual-screen flexibility.
The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile, with just a single 48MP rear camera.
Our choice: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It offers the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.


						

							


Which iPhone has the best battery life? iPhone 18 Pro Max

				
					

				
			
Bigger iPhone means bigger battery.

Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating it for up to 45 hours of video playback. That puts it comfortably ahead of the smaller iPhone 18 Pro and makes battery life one of the strongest reasons to choose the Pro Max.
The iPhone Duo comes surprisingly close, with up to 44 hours of video playback when using its outer 5.4-inch display. However, battery life drops to around 31 hours when using the larger 7.6-inch folding display, so the Pro Max remains the better choice if endurance is your priority.
The iPhone 18 Pro is also excellent, offering up to 36 hours of video playback. That makes it a good compromise if you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max.
Further down the range, the iPhone 17 offers up to 30 hours, making it the best mainstream option for battery life. The iPhone Air manages around 27 hours despite its exceptionally thin design, while the iPhone 17e reaches 26 hours.
The older iPhone 16 trails the current lineup at up to 22 hours of video playback.
Our choice: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear winner. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travellers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.


						

							




Here’s how the current iPhone lineup compares in terms of battery life


ModelVideo Playback (Apple’s rating)Geekbench 4 Test (minutes)Wired Charging (50% time)

iPhone 18 Pro MaxUp to 43 hoursTBC~15 min (60W+)
iPhone DuoUp to 44 hours outer / 31 hours innerTBC~20 min (60W+)
iPhone 18 ProUp to 34 hoursTBC~15 min (60W+)
iPhone 17Up to 30 hours1,053~20 min (40W)
iPhone AirUp to 27 hours880~30 min (20W)
iPhone 17eUp to 26 hours854~30 min (20W)
iPhone 16Up to 24 hours867~30 min (20W)

 






What is the best value iPhone? iPhone 17

				
					

				
			
Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry




The iPhone 17 offers the best overall value for money in Apple’s current lineup. The iPhone 17e is cheaper, but the extra $200/£200 for the iPhone 17 buys a surprisingly large number of worthwhile upgrades.
You get a larger 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display with Always-On support and Dynamic Island, rather than the 17e’s standard 60Hz 6.1-inch screen. The iPhone 17 also adds a second 48MP Ultra Wide camera, including macro photography, along with a better 18MP Centre Stage front camera.
Battery life is stronger too, at up to 30 hours of video playback, compared with 26 hours on the iPhone 17e. You also get stronger graphics performance and a more premium overall experience, while both phones start with a generous 256GB of storage.
At $899/£899, the iPhone 17 also compares very favourably with the older iPhone 16. For just $100/£100 more, you get double the base storage, ProMotion, a larger and brighter display, improved cameras, the newer A19 chip and significantly better battery life.
If your priority is spending as little as possible, choose the iPhone 17e which delivers excellent performance for $699/£699. Or seek out a refurbished iPhone from the Apple Refurbished Store or another place that sells refurbished iPhones.
Our choice: In terms of the features and hardware you get for every pound or dollar spent, the iPhone 17 is the sweet spot. For most buyers, it delivers the best balance of price, performance, cameras, display quality, battery life and longevity without paying for Pro-level features they may never use. Even better if you can find a iPhone 17 deal, then you are really getting a bargain. 


						

							


Best iPhone for gaming: iPhone 18 Pro

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro is the best iPhone for gaming for most people, thanks to its combination of the A20 Pro chip, seven-core GPU and improved vapor-chamber cooling.
The A20 Pro is Apple’s fastest iPhone processor, but the cooling system is just as important for gaming. Better heat management should help the iPhone 18 Pro maintain high performance for longer during demanding games, rather than slowing down as the phone gets hot. Its 6.3-inch 120Hz ProMotion display also provides smooth animation and responsive gameplay without making the phone excessively large or heavy.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max offers essentially the same gaming performance, but adds a much larger 6.9-inch display and significantly longer battery life. That arguably makes it the best choice for serious mobile gamers who value screen size and endurance, although it is heavier and costs more.
The iPhone Duo also uses the A20 Pro and has an enormous 7.6-inch folding display, which could be fantastic for some games, but its weight, price and unconventional form factor make it a more specialised choice.
Our choice: For most gamers, the iPhone 18 Pro offers the best balance of performance, cooling, display quality and portability. It’s the best choice if you prefer a more pocketable device but still want top-tier gaming power.


						

							


Best iPhone for seniors and older users: iPhone 17e

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




For most older users, the iPhone 17e is probably the best choice, because it combines a relatively simple feature set with modern performance, strong battery life and a lower price than Apple’s flagship models.
Its 6.1-inch OLED display is large enough to make text, icons and controls easy to see without making the phone too bulky, while the A19 chip should keep it feeling fast for years. It also supports Apple Intelligence and starts with 256GB of storage, so there’s plenty of room for photos, apps and videos.
The iPhone 17 is a better option for someone who would benefit from a larger and more advanced display. Its 6.3-inch ProMotion screen, Always-On support and higher brightness can make scrolling, reading and outdoor use more comfortable. It also offers stronger battery life and better cameras, although it costs more.
We don’t recommend the iPhone Air, Pro Max or Duo for older users. The Air sacrifices battery life and camera flexibility for thinness, while the Pro Max and Duo are much heavier and considerably more expensive.
Our choice: iPhone 17e is the perfect choice for most older users.


						

							


Best iPhone for kids: iPhone 17e

				
					

				
			
Ida Blix




The iPhone 17e is the best iPhone for most children. As Apple’s most affordable current-generation model, it offers the best balance of price, performance and longevity, while being easier to justify than a flagship model if it gets lost or damaged.
It uses the same A19 chip as the iPhone 17, albeit with one fewer GPU core, so it’s easily fast enough for games, social media, schoolwork and Apple Intelligence. Battery life is strong, the 6.1-inch OLED display is a sensible size for smaller hands, and the 48MP camera is more than capable for everyday photos, even though it lacks an Ultra Wide lens.
The iPhone 17 is the better choice for older teenagers who care more about photography, video or display quality. It adds a 48MP Ultra Wide camera, a better front camera and a larger 6.3-inch ProMotion display, but costs considerably more.
A hand-me-down iPhone is also worth considering. It’s the cheapest option and better for the environment, provided you erase the phone first, create a Child Account through Family Sharing, and configure Screen Time and parental controls before handing it over. Read: How to set up an iPhone for a child. 
Whichever iPhone you choose, those controls matter. In iOS 27, Apple is expanding Screen Time with new category-based Time Allowances, Ask to Browse, more flexible app schedules and improved contact controls. Communication Safety can also detect and blur sensitive, violent or graphic content.
For very young children, an iPad may still be a better first Apple device. By the time they reach 11 or 12 though, an iPhone becomes much more useful for staying in touch.
Our choice: iPhone 17e for most kids; iPhone 17 for older teens who want better cameras and display quality.


						

							


Should you buy an older iPhone? 

				
					

				
			
Macwelt




Buying an older iPhone can be a great way to save money, but the key is choosing a model that still has plenty of useful life ahead of it. Apple typically provides around five to seven years of major iOS updates, with security updates often continuing for longer, so a relatively recent iPhone can remain perfectly usable for years.
We wouldn’t recommend simply buying the cheapest iPhone you can find. Very old models may technically run recent versions of iOS, but performance, battery condition and access to newer features can become increasingly compromised. We currently recommend avoiding anything older than the iPhone 15 Pro because even the iPhone 15 doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. You should definitely avoid models such as the iPhone XS and XR that can no longer run the latest iOS releases.
A refurbished recent-generation iPhone can offer particularly good value. You may be able to buy a former Pro model with better cameras and displays for less than a new entry-level iPhone. Buying from a reputable refurbisher is important, however: check the warranty, battery condition, returns policy and whether genuine replacement parts have been used. Apple’s own refurbished iPhones include a new battery and outer shell and come with a one-year warranty.
Our advice: A discounted or refurbished iPhone 16 or newer should offer an excellent combination of price, features and longevity.

title: Apple reportedly slashes employee AI usage limits amid ‘cost-cutting effort’
content:
Macworld





Apple took its time jumping on the AI bandwagon, announcing Apple Intelligence as late as 2024 (nearly three and a half years after the release of DALL-E, and one and a half after ChatGPT) then delaying some of the platform’s flagship features for years after that. But these days the company is a committed proponent of “truly helpful AI that’s centered around you and your needs,” as it writes on the dedicated Apple Intelligence page on its website.
Product pages for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo extol their ability to handle AI workloads, and similar language is used to market the iMac, iPad mini, Apple Watch Series 12, HomeView, and pretty much every other product Apple sells. Former CEO Tim Cook said AI is critical to Apple’s products back in 2023, while new boss John Ternus told Wired last month that the company is “absolutely going to leverage AI” to build incredible products.
However, as much as it encourages customers to enjoy the benefits of AI, Apple has seemingly soured on excessive use of the technology by its own employees. In a new report, Bloomberg claims the company has begun “reducing employee budgets for artificial intelligence usage as part of a cost-cutting effort.”
Citing anonymous people with knowledge of the change, leaker Mark Gurman says Apple last month reduced the daily AI spending cap for some engineers from $300 to $200, and is planning to make further cuts which could see limits drop as low as $100. “Many groups outside of engineering already face a $100 daily cap, but Apple has considered reducing that limit to as little as $25 for some teams,” Gurman adds. Staff who believe these limits will impede their ability to do their job can ask for an exemption.
The spending limits relate to the tokens used by AI providers to track the volume and nature of usage, and to set fees. Complex, data-intensive tasks such as debugging code may cost more tokens than the lighter usage typical among consumers.
Some Apple employees will therefore need to be more conservative in the data-processing demands they place on AI. But others, apparently, won’t need to change anything about their approach. Gurman’s sources claim that “few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous,” which suggests the savings obtained through the measure will be small.
Aside from those public comments praising the usefulness of AI, this is a surprising stance from a company which in its most recent financial disclosure announced its “best fiscal year ever.” But Apple has long been a company obsessed with spotting and eliminating unnecessary costs, with Cook (who came from an operations background) famous for his ability to optimise a supply chain.
Last month’s initial AI spending cut, while it happened on Ternus’s watch, may have been a decision made, or at least floated, while Cook was still in charge. But the plan to cut deeper shows that Ternus is just as keen as his predecessor on running an efficient company.
And after all, as he said in the Wired interview linked above, “We don’t want to ship AI for AI’s sake. When we’re doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”

title: iPhone Duo guide: Price, specs, availability, problems and reviews
content:
Macworld





Apple’s first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo, went on sale on October 23, but getting hold of one could prove difficult. Preorders opened on October 16 and delivery estimates slipped rapidly, with Macworld’s U.S. tracking showing waits stretching to January 25, 2027 within around half an hour. Apple is still accepting orders and made limited stock available to walk-in customers at Apple Stores in the U.S., U.K. and other selected markets on October 23. 
However, the launch has brought durability concerns, with some early owners reporting cracks and bright lines on the inner display. On October 26, Apple acknowledged an inner-display issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units and advised affected customers to contact AppleCare for a replacement. The cause and failure rate remain unclear. Our iPhone Duo fold problems section below explains Apple’s response and what affected owners should do. The underlying cause of the reported screen cracks has not been confirmed.
The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro. The biggest difference compared to previous iPhones is the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo launched with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. The iOS 27.2 update, released on October 26, adds Apple Pencil (USB-C) support and Edge Light, which uses the display to light your face during video calls.
The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime. Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colors were all anticipated.
iPhone Duo at a glance
Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.
iPhone Duo: Top 10 features


Foldable designBook-style titanium design with precision hinge
Inner display7.6-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
Outer display5.4-inch Super Retina XDR OLED, 120Hz ProMotion
ProcessorA20 Pro, 6-core CPU, 7-core GPU
Neural EngineDual 16-core Neural Engine
AuthenticationTouch ID in side button
Rear cameras48MP Main + 48MP Ultra Wide
BatteryDual batteries; up to 44 hours video on outer screen
ConnectivityC2 modem, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, second-gen UWB
Storage256GB, 512GB, 1TB or 2TB

 






iPhone Duo release date: When did it launch?
Apple announced the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Sales began on October 23, following preorders on October 16.
The October 23 launch covers more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S. and U.K., with another 28 markets following on October 30. The Duo will also be available through Apple Stores, selected carriers and authorized retailers, although availability varies by market.
Buy iPhone Duo at Apple U.S. 
Buy iPhone Duo at Apple U.K. 
$1999 at  Apple						
					


						

							


Has the iPhone Duo sold out? 
Initial delivery allocations sold out rapidly. Delivery dates have now slipped to late January 2027. 
As of October 23, Apple was quoting January 22, 2027 for delivery of the 256GB iPhone Duo in the U.S. and January 25, 2027 in the U.K. Estimates can change and depend on the configuration and delivery location.
Apple offered limited iPhone Duo stock to walk-in customers when sales began on October 23, but that stock quickly ran out. There are iPhone stock-checking services that may help you locate stock near you. Apple Inventory Check monitors Apple Store availability in various countries, including the U.S. and U.K., while TrackaLacker covers selected online retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart. Some notification features require registration or payment.
Apple described preorder demand as “nothing short of extraordinary” and said it was working to get devices to customers as quickly as possible.
Supply constraints may also contribute to the backlog. A late-September report claimed that Apple and its manufacturing partners were experiencing low production yields. Long delivery waits therefore reflect the balance between demand and available supply, rather than revealing how many phones Apple has sold.


						

							


iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			


Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.
The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. 
According to iFixit’s report on Apple’s U.S. repair pricing, replacing the inner screen’s cover layer costs $49 without AppleCare+, or a $19 service fee with AppleCare+. This replaces only the top cover layer. Repairing damage to the inner display itself costs substantially more: $999 without AppleCare+, or a $99 service fee with AppleCare+. If damage is experienced and found to be a manufacturing fault, Apple may accept the device for repair under warranty at no cost. 
The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

				
					

				
			A closed iPhone Duo.

Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.
Action button and Camera Control
There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.
However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.
Accessories
Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable: 
The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129
Apple’s standard case leaves the hinge exposed, while the Folio with Kickstand provides hinge protection.
Both became available to order on October 16. And there are plenty more of the best cases for iPhone Duo in our test reviews.


						

							


iPhone Duo problems: Screen cracks and hinge concerns
Some early iPhone Duo owners have reported cracks along the inner display’s fold, sometimes accompanied by bright lines across the screen. One Australian owner said the damage appeared after around six hours and fewer than 20 openings, and reported receiving an immediate replacement at an Apple Store. These are owner reports; the cause and extent of the problem remain unclear.
Apple acknowledged the issue on October 26, saying it affects a small number of iPhone Duo units. The company advises customers experiencing inner-display problems to contact AppleCare for a replacement. Apple has not announced a formal repair program or confirmed the underlying cause. As reported on November 2, Apple has also circulated diagnostic guidance to Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers. Read our report on the Duo’s display and hinge problems.
iFixit’s teardown offers a possible explanation: its 3D hinge model places reported damage near a transition between the flex-cable opening and central display support. One simulation shows how a support that fails to retract sufficiently could press against the folding screen.
Apple published an iPhone Duo hinge troubleshooting guide on October 23. It covers devices that do not open or close fully, unexpected noises, loose or damaged hinges, and enclosure damage affecting the mechanism.
Apple says there are no software remedies for hinge problems, so restarting, updating or restoring the phone is unnecessary. Its service procedure calls for inspection and, if the problem remains unresolved, replacement of the inner display assembly. Owners experiencing problems should contact Apple or an authorized service provider for assessment.


						

							


How repairable is the iPhone Duo?
iFixit awarded the Duo a provisional repairability score of 5/10, its highest for a foldable at the time. It praised the removable outer display and electrically released batteries, but found inner-display and hinge repairs difficult. The score reflects some accessible components, but is provisional pending replacement-parts availability.
Its fluorescent-powder experiment also found particles reaching the hinge, but this does not establish the cause of owners’ screen failures.


						

							


Face ID, Touch ID and the notch

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.
Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.
The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.
The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.
Future Duo models could restore Face ID. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple has tested iPhone Duo 2 prototypes with an under-display Face ID sensor and camera on the outer screen. However, he suggests the technology could arrive with either the second or third generation, so its inclusion in the next model remains uncertain.


						

							




iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

				
					

				
			
There are two cameras on the rear.

Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:


CameraResolutionEquivalent focal lengthAperture

Fusion Main48MP26mmf/1.6
2x crop from Main12MP52mmf/1.6
Fusion Ultra Wide48MP13mmf/2.2
Outer front camera12MP—f/2.2
Inner FaceTime cameraApple does not specify resolution—f/1.8

 



The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo
Duo Preview
The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.
Smart Take and Kid Cue
Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.
Two-screen shooting
The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.
Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.


						

							


Rear cameras

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.
The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.
That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.
In his first-day testing, Macworld’s Jason Cross found the Duo’s Main camera fell behind the iPhone 18 Pro in low light, although he was pleased with the Ultra Wide camera. The Duo also lacks the Pro’s shutter-speed adjustment and histogram, while retaining white balance and manual focus with focus peaking.
Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.
Front cameras
On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.
Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.
However, image quality is a compromise. In Macworld’s testing, we found that the under-display camera produced poor detail and dynamic range. It is adequate for video calls, but for better selfies, it’s preferable to use the rear cameras with the outer display as a viewfinder.
iPhone Duo video features
The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.
Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.
The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.
Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.


						

							


iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

				
					

				
			
Watch video on the screen.

Apple




The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.
The A20 Pro includes:
6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
Dual 16-core Neural Engine
Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays
Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.
Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.


						

							


iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?
Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.
Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models. 
Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.
Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.


						

							


iPhone Duo connectivity

				
					

				
			
Folded iPhone Duo. 

Britta O’Boyle




Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.
It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.
The N1 wireless networking chip provides:
Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
Bluetooth 6
Thread networking
The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.
The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.
It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.
iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.
Satellite capabilities include:
Emergency SOS via satellite
Roadside Assistance via satellite
Find My via satellite
Messages via satellite


						

							


Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?
Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.
Apple rates battery life at:
Up to 24 hours of typical use
Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
Up to 31 hours using the inner display
Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display
Early reviewers reported different battery experiences. CNET found the Duo comfortably lasted through a busy day, while The Verge questioned whether it could manage a full day of heavy use. These observations reflect different usage patterns and testing methods, so they should not be treated as directly comparable results or replacements for Apple’s playback ratings above.
After using the Duo as her main phone for a week, Macworld contributor Britta O’Boyle generally finished her mixed-use days with around 25 percent battery remaining. In her experience, it outlasted the smaller iPhone 18 Pro but fell slightly short of the Pro Max. These are everyday-use observations rather than directly comparable laboratory benchmarks.
Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.
Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.
Britta O’Boyle’s charging test broadly matched Apple’s claim: using a 60W adapter, she reached approximately 50 percent from empty in around 20 minutes.
Our iPhone Duo reviewer, Jason Cross, found that battery life depended heavily on which display he used. Frequent gaming or video editing on the inner screen could require charging by mid-afternoon, while more folded use left plenty of charge at bedtime. Unfortunately, Macworld’s standard battery benchmark app crashed on launch, so his review contains no directly comparable laboratory battery result.
MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.
In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.


						

							




iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?
The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.
Prices are:


StoragePrice

256GB$1,999/£1,999
512GB$2,199/£2,199
1TB$2,599/£2,599
2TB$3,199/£3,199

 



The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.


iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.
That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.
Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.


						

							


iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle





The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.
App compatibility varies considerably. Macworld’s Jason Cross identified three broad experiences: older apps with fixed layouts and black borders; apps updated for iOS 27 that resize across the displays; and fully Duo-optimized apps that adapt to its different positions. After some initial issues, Outlook has been updated and now has a Duo-optimized layout that makes better use of the inner display.
App support is improving, however. Netflix, Fantastical, MLB and Asphalt Legends were among the apps Apple highlighted at launch, and optimized apps carry a “Made for iPhone Duo“ badge on their App Store product pages. You can also consult the crowdsourced Works on Duo database to check how individual apps use the Duo’s displays before buying.
StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.
Apple Pencil (USB-C) support arrived with iOS 27.2 on October 26, allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display. Update through Settings > General > Software Update to access the feature.
The update also adds Edge Light, which uses the display to illuminate your face during video calls. Other iOS 27.2 additions include improvements to Siri AI’s conversation recall and personal context, plus contextual Suggestions in Messages. Read our guide to the iOS 27.2 update.


						

							


iPhone Duo review: What did Macworld think?
In Macworld’s full iPhone Duo review, Jason Cross praises the nano-texture inner display, fast performance and thoughtful layouts in optimized apps. 
However, many everyday apps remain awkward to use, while the cameras and Touch ID introduce further compromises. 
Our verdict: An exciting device to explore, but one he cannot yet recommend buying.


						

							


Should you buy the iPhone Duo?

				
					

				
			
Britta O’Boyle




Our advice is to wait, principally because too many popular apps still work poorly on the Duo. Before buying an iPhone Duo, check whether the apps you rely on have layouts designed for its displays.
Additionally, at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 
Durability is another consideration. On October 26, Apple acknowledged an inner-display issue affecting a small number of iPhone Duo units and advised affected customers to contact AppleCare for a replacement. The cause and failure rate remain unclear. If first-generation reliability concerns you, consider waiting for further investigation and longer-term testing before spending $1,999/£1,999.
For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the better-value iPhone 18 Pro Max is the best iPhone.
Also read: When is the best time to buy an iPhone and our iPhone Buying Guide.

title: HomeView Code Suggests Future Support for AI Chatbot Apps, Anti-Spoofing Protection
content:
Code discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests Apple is laying the groundwork for chatbot apps on its upcoming HomeView smart home hub, according to the code investigator known as pdfu.


The software HomeView uses to display apps from a connected iPhone or iPad is said to have gained a "Conversational Apps" category in the latest beta. The update also reportedly adds preparations for two-way audio routing, session management, and interruptions, but pdfu notes that it is "still not fully wired up." 

suggested on Sunday that chatbot apps might follow based on an unused flag in HomeView's software.

Anti-Spoofing Protection

In a separate finding, pdfu also discovered that HomeView includes anti-spoofing protection. Apparently, after three spoof attempts for a profile, the user must authenticate with an iPhone to see personal data, and the protection is enabled in HomeView software 27.2. 

Apple is also said to be working on a lockout cooldown system, similar to what happens when you enter the wrong passcode on an iPhone. A first lockout can be cleared immediately, but a second lockout brings a one-hour wait, a third a four-hour wait, and a fourth (or any further) lockout an eight-hour wait.

pdfu adds that the lockout cooldown periods are still in development, so for now any lockout can be cleared immediately by authenticating with an iPhone. Apple hasn't described either feature in its press materials.

HomeView Launches Next Week

HomeView launches on November 13 for $299, in both desktop and wall-mounted versions. Here's what Apple has announced so far:

7-inch Liquid Retina display, in a tabletop model with a speaker base and a wall-mounted model.

Face recognition for up to six users, each with a personal Home Screen with apps and widgets.

Siri AI, with conversations that continue in the Siri app on other Apple devices.

Personal content from Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My, shown when the enrolled user is recognized and their iPhone or iPad is nearby and recently unlocked.

Faces including Photos, Flow, Snoopy, Home Modular, and Home Camera.

Apple Music, Podcasts, News, and Apple TV, plus compatible third-party audio and video apps.

Handoff from iPhone, and multiroom audio with HomePod, HomePod mini, and AirPlay speakers.

FaceTime with Center Stage, Messages by voice or keyboard, and Intercom.

Step-by-step recipes from the web with hands-free timers.

Smart home controls, including a Home Camera face that shows up to nine live camera feeds.

With a supported iCloud+ subscription, recognition of people, pets, packages, and vehicles from compatible cameras.

Smoke and carbon monoxide alarm sound detection.

Support for Apple Home Collection accessories, other "Works with Apple Home" accessories, and Matter.

HomeView won't have an App Store. However, as we reported last month, it shows CarPlay-style third-party audio and video apps from a connected iPhone or iPad. HomeView isn't on sale in the European Union because Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS there, and Apple says it is still working with the EU to find a path forward to make it available in the bloc.

title: These Finder tips will make you a Mac pro
content:
Macworld





The Finder in macOS is where you spend the most time when using your Mac. It is the most important tool for managing files and folders; it’s the basis for installing and launching apps; it’s where you can manage iPhones and iPads; and a lot more. It’s the foundation for the macOS interface and for using your Mac hardware.
Many Mac users have been using the Finder every day for decades, often without making full use of its capabilities or customizing it to suit their own needs. You should make the most of your UI experience. Here are ten tips on how to get more out of the Finder.
Customize the toolbar
This is a very simple thing to do, but hardly anyone does. You should adjust the  Finder toolbar to suit your own needs. To do this, open a Finder window and right-click on the toolbar. You’ll see the Customize Toolbar option in the context menu. Select it, and a window will appear with additional functions and tools. You can click and drag icons to where you want them in the toolbar.
The AirDrop icon, for example, is useful if you transfer files often: once it’s been added to the Finder, you simply select an item and send it straight away. The buttons for burning blank discs, ejecting media, and accessing servers can also be useful, depending on your needs.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can also easily change the order of the icons. Simply click on one while holding down the Command key. To remove it from the toolbar, simply drag it out.
Quick Commands for photo editing and your own scripts
Quick Actions are small tools that you can access via the context menu (the menu that appears when you right-click an item). They allow you to quickly convert PNG to JPEG or create a PDF, for example.
Six system services are provided by default, though the options available in the context menu depend on the selected file type. For example, if you right-click on a video, you can access a function to trim the video. This is quicker and easier than using QuickTime Player.
For photos, you can quickly convert them to other formats such as JPEG; you can combine several PDFs into a single PDF file using Create PDF; rotate a photo; and remove the background from a photo (though this doesn’t always work). For image files and PDFs, there’s also the option to add annotations. This opens a window with the tools familiar from Preview, allowing you to add lines, red arrows, and other annotations.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can enable and disable these useful extensions under General > Login Items & Extensions > System Services. To do this, click on the ‘i’ icon there.
There’s even a way to add your own Quick Actions: to do this, simply select ‘Quick Action’ as the file type in Automator and create a workflow – such as resizing a photo to a specific width. Once created, the workflow is immediately available via the context menu.
Rename multiple files
You don’t need to resort to a tool like Renamer to rename dozens of files or folders. The Finder also has a built-in function for renaming files. However, it’s somewhat hidden.
To access the feature, select multiple files and choose Rename from the context menu. If you selected just a single file, you can only change the name within the Finder; the file will be selected for you automatically. However, if you’ve selected multiple files, a separate new window opens with several options.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Here you can choose from several renaming options; you can add text, replace text, or rename all files according to a new format. When replacing text, simply enter the original text and the new text in the two fields. When adding text, you can choose to add it at the beginning or the end, as a prefix or suffix.
The Format option is more complex, offering three choices: here you can choose between two numbering styles and adding the current date.
Manage the clipboards
Starting with macOS Tahoe, old clipboard contents can be saved by the system on request and are searchable via Spotlight. You’ll need to enable this feature first via the Spotlight system setting. You can also select a retention period; options are 8 hours, 30 minutes, and 7 days.
Once enabled, you can enter a search term into Spotlight to search the clipboard text. Alongside other results, you’ll then see a list of previous clipboard entries, marked with two small boxes. You can also press Command+4 or select Clipboard after opening Spotlight.
You can valso iew the current clipboard select Edit > Show Clipboard from the menu bar in Finder, and the current clipboard will be displayed in a simple window.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Hide all items on the Desktop
Apple now offers so many options for the Desktop and Dock that some people lose track of them all. For a long time, I overlooked the fact that the Desktop & Dock system setting can hide all items on the desktop completely.
To do this, go to the Desktop & Dock system settings and, under Show items, untick the box next to On the Desktop. You can later show all folders and files again using the same function.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




List invisible files and folders
The Mac actually has countless invisible folders and files on your system. Most are used by the system and are best left hidden, otherwise, your folders can quickly become cluttered. Sometimes, invisible files are left behind when you uninstall an app or delete a file.
All you need to do is press Command+Shift+. to see invisible files.  The first time you press the key combination, you see all hidden files and folders in the selected folder. Press it again, and they’ll disappear again.
Hide files or folders
You can make a file or folder invisible via Terminal: enter the command chflags hidden and add the path–drag and drop the file or folder into the Terminal window to do this.
Connect to a server
The Finder is also responsible for allowing you to connect via the network: to other Macs, the company server or even a Fritzbox with NAS functionality. Available servers are often listed automatically in the Finder under Network. You can connect manually via Go > Connect to Server. 
Even FTP is supported, but you can only download data. Uploads are not possible, and FTP servers using the SFTP or FTPS protocols are not supported. However, the FTP function is not always reliable and has often caused problems. It is not without reason that many experienced users prefer to use an FTP client such as Cyberduck for every FTP connection.
Make better use of Smart Folders
Smart Folders are very powerful, but unfortunately can be too fiddly. These ingenious folders are essentially saved search queries that update dynamically. You can save these folders once created and conveniently pin them to the sidebar. By default, however, the Finder links all search criteria using only simple AND conditions, as is familiar from Spotlight or the Google search engine.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




But the folder becomes truly smart with so-called Boolean operators. For example, when you’re looking for all image files but also all video files, or all files that are neither image files nor video files. (This might sound like a fiddly logic puzzle to you right now, but it can be very useful!)
Apple has hidden this option a little, presumably so as not to overwhelm beginners. First, create a smart folder as usual, for example, via File > New Smart Folder. Then click the + icon, and you can define the criteria for the items you want to appear in the folder. Click the + icon to add more definitions. Click the Save button to set the Smart Folder, and then when you open the folder, it will show all the items that fit the criteria you defined.

title: Got an iPhone Duo on Launch Day? Today Could Be Your Last Chance to Return It
content:
If you bought an iPhone Duo on launch day and are having second thoughts about keeping Apple's first foldable iPhone, today could be your last chance to return it for a refund.


Apple officially launched the iPhone Duo on Friday, October 23, so the standard 14-day return window for customers who purchased and received the device that day expires on Friday, November 6.

Apple's U.S. return policy, customers have 14 calendar days from receiving a product to return it, whether they purchased it online or at an Apple retail store. A similar standard return period applies in the UK and across much of the rest of Europe.

Apple's Canadian return policy, buyers have 15 calendar days from receiving their device to initiate a return, so if you got your device on launch day then you have until Saturday, November 7 to return it.

UK and EU Online Customers Have More Time to Send It Back

There's an important distinction to note if you're in the UK or the European Union and you purchased your iPhone Duo online. Under consumer protection laws, you have 14 days from receiving the device to notify Apple that you intend to return it. Once you've made that notification, you have a further 14 days to send the device back or arrange a collection.

November 20 to dispatch it. This also applies to devices ordered online and collected at an Apple Store. However, if you actually purchased your device directly at a physical Apple Store – which probably means you waited in a separate line to collections – then you generally need to return it within the initial 14-day window.

Note that the November 6 deadline doesn't apply to everyone who pre-ordered the iPhone Duo. Apple's return period is calculated from when customers received their devices, rather than when they placed their orders, so if your iPhone Duo arrived after launch day, you have more time to return it for a refund – if that's your preference.

What to Know Before Returning Your iPhone Duo

Apple asks customers to return their devices with the original packaging and included accessories. Also, remember to disable Find My for the iPhone Duo before returning the device. Returns can be initiated through Apple's online Order Status page or, in the US, at an Apple retail store.

Keep in mind that these policies apply only to purchases made directly from Apple – if you bought an iPhone Duo through a carrier or third-party retailer, you'll be subject to that seller's return policy.

title: You don’t need a $3,000 MacBook to get Live Activities in your menu bar
content:
Macworld





One of the big selling points of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED is its inclusion of a Dynamic Island. The camera is just a tiny bit lower and surrounded by display, so instead of a notch, you get an island that’s smaller but just as capable as the iPhone’s. When you run apps with Live Activities on the new laptop, they’ll populate the Dynamic Island, and you can tap or click on them to expand it. 
What iPhone users have enjoyed for years finally comes to Apple’s most expensive laptop. But it turns out, the Live Activities feature is coming to all Macs. In the macOS 27.3 beta, every Mac gets Live Activities. It’s just for some of Apple’s apps right now, such as Music and Clock, and some system functions like Screen Recording.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Live Activities in macOS 27.3 will appear in the menu bar as small ovals to the left of your icons, just as if there were a camera hole up there. When expanded, a small arrow appears that can be clicked to minimize it (see above). If you run several at a time, they’ll appear as separate instances next to each other. 
Third-party developers can now start implementing Live Activities in their macOS apps, which was already announced. However, what we thought was just in anticipation of the PROLED MacBook Pro turns out to be a new, useful feature for everyone.

title: iPhone buying guide 2026: Which iPhone should you buy?

With the iPhone Duo now on sale, choosing an iPhone now includes a new question: do you want a conventional phone or one that folds open into a larger display? Apple’s first foldable joins an already extensive lineup, but the newest – and most expensive – model won’t be the best choice for everyone.
Your decision will depend on your budget and what matters most to you, whether that’s camera quality, battery life, a bigger screen or a phone that fits comfortably in your pocket. Older models can also offer excellent value, with some particularly attractive U.K. deals on the discontinued iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max.
In this guide, we compare every iPhone currently available from Apple, covering prices, cameras, displays, performance, battery life, durability, design and storage. We also explain the compromises to consider before choosing the Duo and when an older model could be a better buy.
If you simply want to know which models we recommend, head to our Best iPhone recommendations. For a closer look at individual models, read our full iPhone reviews, linked below.

How to choose an iPhone
To help you narrow down the right iPhone model, we’ll look at the key questions that matter most when choosing an iPhone, including which has the best camera, battery life, display and performance, how much storage you need, and which model offers the best value.


Which iPhone has the best camera? 

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max have the best camera systems of any current iPhone. Both use the same triple-48MP rear camera setup, so there is no photographic advantage to choosing the larger Pro Max unless you also want its bigger display and longer battery life.
The headline upgrade is the 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, a first for the iPhone. You can switch between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4.0, giving you more direct control over depth of field and low-light shooting. The Pro models also add a 48MP Ultra Wide and 48MP Telephoto camera, with 4x native telephoto and an 8x optical-quality zoom option. Apple also provides manual controls for aperture, shutter speed, white balance and histogram viewing, plus ProRAW, ProRes RAW and Apple Log 2 support.
The iPhone 17 remains an excellent camera phone for most people. It has a 48MP Main camera and 48MP Ultra Wide camera, plus a 12MP optical-quality 2x option cropped from the Main sensor. It also gains the 18MP Center Stage front camera, which can automatically reframe shots and supports Dual Capture. What you miss compared with the Pro models is the dedicated Telephoto lens, longer zoom range and more advanced pro photo and video controls.
The iPhone Duo also has two 48MP rear cameras, with Main and Ultra Wide lenses plus a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main sensor. Its folding design introduces some unusual camera features, including Duo Preview and Smart Take, but it lacks the dedicated Telephoto and variable-aperture Main camera found on the Pro models.
In our initial testing, the Duo’s Main camera fell behind the iPhone 18 Pro in low light, while its Ultra Wide impressed. The inner selfie camera produced noticeably soft, heavily processed images; using the rear Main camera with the outer-screen preview is a better option for selfies. The Duo offers white balance and manual focus with focus peaking, but lacks shutter-speed adjustment and a histogram.
The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e are the least versatile current models, because each has only a single 48MP rear camera. Both can produce a 12MP optical-quality 2x view from the Main sensor, but neither has an Ultra Wide camera. The Air does at least get the newer 18MP Center Stage front camera, while the 17e retains a 12MP TrueDepth camera.
The older iPhone 16 sits somewhere in between, with a 48MP Main camera and 12MP Ultra Wide, plus the same 2x optical-quality crop from the Main sensor. It is still a capable camera phone, but the iPhone 17 improves the Ultra Wide to 48MP and upgrades the front camera.
Our recommendation: If photography and video are your priority, buy the iPhone 18 Pro. It gives you exactly the same camera system as the Pro Max for less money and in a more manageable size.

iPhone camera specifications compared
Here’s how the current iPhone cameras compare. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max share the same triple-camera system, including the variable-aperture Main camera and 4x/8x Telephoto setup, while the iPhone 17 steps down to dual 48MP Main and Ultra Wide cameras. The iPhone Air and 17e are less versatile, each using a single 48MP rear camera. Most newer models also feature Apple’s 18MP Center Stage front camera with automatic reframing and Dual Capture, while the iPhone 17e retains a 12MP TrueDepth camera and the iPhone Duo uses separate outer and inner front cameras.

Which iPhone has the best battery life? 

				
					

				
			
Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro Max has the best battery life of any current iPhone, with Apple rating eSIM-only models for up to 45 hours of video playback, compared with 43 hours for versions with a physical SIM slot. Its larger battery and efficient A20 Pro chip make endurance a major reason to choose it over the smaller iPhone 18 Pro. However, modem hardware varies by region: according to iFixit’s teardown, the U.S. iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a Qualcomm modem, while Pro Max models sold elsewhere and all iPhone 18 Pro models use Apple’s C2 modem.
Apple rates the iPhone Duo for up to 44 hours of video playback on its outer display and 31 hours on its inner display. Early reviewers reported differing experiences: CNET found it comfortably lasted through a busy day, while The Verge questioned its endurance under heavy use. 
In Macworld contributor Britta O’Boyle’s week using the Duo as her main phone, she finished most days with around 25 percent battery remaining. In her mixed use, it outlasted the iPhone 18 Pro but fell short of the Pro Max. She also reached roughly 50 percent charge from empty in 20 minutes using a 60W adapter. 
Macworld’s iPhone Duo testing highlighted how much endurance depends on which screen you use. Heavy gaming or video editing on the inner display could require charging by mid-afternoon, while predominantly folded use left plenty of charge at day’s end. Our usual battery benchmark app crashed on launch, so we don’t yet have directly comparable benchmark results for the Duo
If you want strong battery life without carrying the much larger and heavier Pro Max, the iPhone 18 Pro is an excellent compromise at up to 36 hours, while the iPhone 17 remains the best mainstream option at up to 30 hours.
Our recommendation: If battery life matters above everything else, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is the clear choice. Its combination of a 45-hour rating, huge 6.9-inch display and Pro-level performance makes it particularly well suited to heavy users, travelers and anyone who wants to get through a long day without worrying about charging.
